events.text: Below the village, an abandoned watermill on the Ying River has not worked in ten years. Yet every morning there is fresh flour on its stone floor, and the villagers say a ghost is grinding. You are the only one curious enough to go and look.
events.arc: The Mill That Grinds at Night

effects.log: At midnight the wheel creaks into motion. A small figure with a lantern shuffles in below you. You hold your breath until dawn.

choices.text: Leave a coin on the millstone

effects.log: In the morning the coin is gone and there is a bun in its place, still warm.

choices.text: Tell the villagers it is rats

effects.log: Nobody believes you, but they laugh, and the ghost talk dies down a little.

events.text: You go back to the night mill. The ghost is an old woman, bent nearly double, who cannot sleep since her husband died and grinds grain for the whole village because the sound reminds her of him. She makes you swear not to tell.
events.arc: The Mill That Grinds at Night

effects.log: You push until your arms burn. She talks about her husband the whole time, and laughs twice.
You keep it. The village goes on leaving offerings for its ghost, and the old woman goes on eating them.

events.text: The old woman of the night mill has died in her sleep, peacefully. The village holds a funeral for her and a separate, very nervous ceremony for the ghost. In the mill you find a sack of flour with your name scratched on it.
events.arc: The Mill That Grinds at Night

choices.text: Tell the village the truth at last

effects.log: They are quiet. Then the miller's son weeps, and the next morning he repairs the wheel. It turns by day now.

choices.text: Bake with the flour and say nothing

effects.log: The bread is the best you have ever eaten. Some secrets are better kept warm.

events.text: On a mountain near Songshan there is a stair of ten thousand steps, every one worn hollow by pilgrims. Halfway up, an old monk sweeps the same three steps over and over. When you pass, he says: "Count them on the way down."

choices.text: Ask the monk why three steps

effects.log: "They are the ones people sit on to give up," he says, and keeps sweeping.

choices.text: Climb to the top without stopping

effects.log: Your legs shake for three days. At the top there is only a small shrine and a very good view.
You go down. Somewhere above you, a broom keeps its patient rhythm.

events.text: You come back to the Ten Thousand Steps and, as the monk said, count them on the way down. There are not ten thousand. There are nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven. The three swept steps are not counted, because they are not steps at all.

effects.log: You sit where people give up. The wind is gentle there. You understand, a little, why the monk sweeps them clean.

choices.text: Find the trick in the stone

ok.log: They are three flat slabs of an older stair, laid by somebody who wanted travellers to rest.

fail.log: You crawl around the slabs for an hour and find nothing but ants.

events.text: The old monk of the stair is gone; a young novice sweeps the three steps now, badly, scattering the leaves. He looks up at you and says that his teacher left word: the next person who sits on the three steps should be shown how to sweep.

effects.log: You sweep together all morning. By noon he is doing it properly, and the path is clear.

choices.text: Take the broom yourself for a season

effects.log: You sweep a whole autumn. Your footwork grows quiet and patient, like the monk's.

choices.text: Leave the broom with the novice

effects.log: You bow to the steps and go. The novice keeps scattering leaves, cheerfully.

events.text: The Yellow River has dropped lower than anyone can remember, and out of the mud near a ferry landing rises the bronze lip of a temple bell big enough to stand inside. When the wind blows across it, it hums.
events.arc: The Bell in the Yellow River

effects.log: You dig all day and uncover an inscription: the name of a town that the river swallowed three hundred years ago.
It rings once, deep and long. Every dog for ten li howls. The ferryman glares at you.
The river will cover it again soon enough. You go on your way.

events.text: Word of the drowned bell has spread. Now a merchant wants to haul it out and sell the bronze, and the old people of the ferry landing say the bell belongs to the town under the river, whose people still ring it on festival nights.
events.arc: The Bell in the Yellow River

effects.log: You stand on the bell until the merchant gives up. The old people bring you dumplings for a week.

choices.text: Help the merchant and take a share

effects.log: The bell comes out in a crane of ropes and oxen. Your share is good silver. The old people do not look at you.

choices.text: Find a deal that suits both

ok.log: The merchant pays to rehang the bell in the ferry temple instead. Everyone is a little unhappy, and so it is fair.

fail.log: Both sides shout at you and you leave with mud on your boots.

events.text: The river has risen again. On the night of the Lantern Festival you are by the ferry landing when, from far under the brown water, a bell begins to ring. Out on the river, small lights rise to the surface one by one and drift downstream.
events.arc: The Bell in the Yellow River

choices.text: Float a lantern of your own

effects.log: Yours drifts out among the others and does not sink. The bell rings once more, as if in answer.

choices.text: Sit and listen until the bell stops

effects.log: It rings until dawn. You go home with the sound in your bones and a quiet in your qi.

events.text: In the ruins of an old palace outside the city, hundreds of cats live among the broken pillars, fat and lazy and plainly fed by someone. A one-eyed tom watches you from a stone lion's head as if you owe him rent.
events.arc: The Cats of the Old Capital

effects.log: Within moments you are wearing cats. The one-eyed tom takes the largest piece and allows you to stay.
You wait. At dusk a eunuch so old he walks with two canes comes through the gate with a basket.
A dozen cats follow you everywhere, judging you. You find nothing but broken tiles.

events.text: The old eunuch of the ruined palace tells you the cats are the descendants of a dowager empress's favourites, and he has fed them for sixty years because she told him to and nobody ever told him to stop. He is worried about who will feed them after him.
events.arc: The Cats of the Old Capital

choices.text: Promise to look in on them

effects.log: He gives you his basket. It is much heavier than it looks.
He tells you stories of the palace for an afternoon, all of them about cats.

events.text: The old eunuch has died. You arrive at the ruined palace to find a crowd of cats waiting at the gate at feeding time, and the one-eyed tom sitting in the empty basket, looking at you.
events.arc: The Cats of the Old Capital

effects.log: You feed them. The tom climbs on your shoulder and stays there all the way home. You have a cat now, apparently.

choices.text: Find a temple to take them in

effects.log: The nuns of a nearby temple agree, after you carry a hundred cats there in baskets. You are scratched all over and happy.

events.text: In a hidden valley north of Luoyang, someone has planted ten thousand peonies. Among them kneels a hermit in a straw hat who was, the rumours say, a sword master of terrible fame, before he put the sword down and picked up a trowel.

effects.log: "Weed that row," he says. You weed it. He says nothing else all day, and you have the oddest feeling you were taught something.
He hands you a trowel instead of a sword. You do not understand, and he does not explain.
You stay until sunset. The colours do something to your qi that no meditation ever has.

events.text: The peony hermit lets you work in the valley for a season. You notice that he never cuts a stem with a blade; he snaps each one at the exact point where it wants to break. One day he hands you the shears and watches.

ok.log: You feel the stem's grain and it parts like water. The hermit grunts, which is high praise.

fail.log: You hack. The peony droops. The hermit sighs like a mountain.

effects.log: "Good," he says. "A blade is only polite in the right hands." You are not sure whether that was praise.

events.text: A band of young swordsmen arrives at the peony valley looking for the famous master, to make a name by beating him. The hermit keeps weeding. They draw their swords among the flowers.

choices.text: Step in front of the flowers

ok.log: You drive them off with a stem of peony in your hand, the way he taught you. Not one flower is broken.

fail.log: They knock you into the flowerbed. The hermit stands, and they leave very fast without being told.

choices.text: Ask the hermit to show them

effects.log: He picks up a trowel. A moment later all six swords are planted in the soil, point down. The young men leave quietly.

events.text: Near the old imperial tombs you meet two tomb robbers having a furious argument over a map. One says the treasure is under the turtle statue, the other says it is under the horse. They ask you to settle it.

effects.log: The turtle man cheers. The horse man sulks. They both start digging and do not notice you leave.
The horse man wins. They dig all night. You hear them still arguing at dawn.

choices.text: Report them to the tomb guards

effects.log: The guards thank you and chase them for a li. The robbers escape, shouting rude things about you.

events.text: You meet the two tomb robbers again on the road, covered in mud and furious at each other. Under the statue they found only a stone tablet that says: "Wrong statue." They show it to you, and both blame you.

effects.log: On the back, in small characters: "Also wrong: the other one." The robbers stare at each other and start laughing.
You run. They are too tired to chase you, and throw the tablet after you instead.

events.text: The two tomb robbers have given up robbing. They now run a teahouse beside the tombs that sells "genuine tomb relics", every one of them made the week before by the turtle man's cousin. They offer you a free cup and a share of the business.

effects.log: The tea is honest, at least. They tell you stories about every tomb in the province.
You put in some silver. A year later a cart of profit arrives with a note: "Not a relic."

choices.text: Tell them to sell honest tea only

effects.log: They grumble, then do it. Business improves. They name a cup after you.

events.text: A small shrine on a hill once ruled by bandits is full of offerings: coins, rice, little wooden swords. The god it honours has no name, only a carving of a woman holding a ladle. Travellers say that if you are robbed on this road, she feeds you.

effects.log: You leave rice. The wind in the pines sounds briefly like someone stirring a pot.

choices.text: Ask the locals who she was

effects.log: Nobody knows. She has been here longer than the bandits, and longer than the road.
The road goes on. You are not robbed. You are also not fed.

events.text: On the road below Bandit Hill you find a merchant family robbed of everything, sitting in the dust. At dusk a woman you have never seen comes down the hill with a pot of porridge and a ladle, feeds them, and walks back up into the dark.

effects.log: You find only the shrine, and in front of it the pot, still warm, and the ladle, washed.

choices.text: Stay with the family until morning

effects.log: You walk them to the next town. They swear to rebuild the shrine one day.

events.text: The merchant family you walked to safety have become rich, and they have kept their word: the shrine on Bandit Hill is now a small temple with a kitchen, where any traveller can eat for free. They have carved your face, very badly, beside the woman with the ladle.

effects.log: The porridge tastes exactly like the pot you found at night. You eat two bowls.

choices.text: Ask them to take your carving down

effects.log: They refuse. You visit it sometimes. It looks nothing like you, which is a relief.

events.text: At harvest time the Central Plains turn into a sea of gold, and you walk into it until the village is gone and there is only wheat and sky. In the middle of a field, a scarecrow is wearing a very fine silk robe.

effects.log: It is embroidered with cranes and very old. In the sleeve is a letter, unopened, addressed to nobody.
The farmer is glad of the hands. You eat a huge supper and sleep in the straw.
You watch the clouds for an hour and feel, for once, exactly the right size.

events.text: You come back for the scarecrow's letter and ask the farmer about the robe. He says his grandfather found it on a dead horse after a war, and the scarecrow has been wearing it ever since because it scares the crows better than rags.

effects.log: It is a love letter, never sent, from a soldier to someone named Plum Blossom. It is very bad poetry, and very sincere.
You put it back in the sleeve. The crows go on being scared.

events.text: At a teahouse in the next town, an old, old woman everyone calls Granny Plum tells anyone who will listen that her soldier never wrote to her, not once, before he died in the war.

effects.log: She reads it four times. Then she laughs until she cries. "It is terrible," she says. "He always was."
You read the terrible poetry to the whole teahouse. Nobody laughs. Granny Plum holds your hand.

events.text: On a peak of Mount Song where no path goes, you find a weiqi board cut into the living rock, with a game half played. The stones are black and white river pebbles, and moss has grown over half of them. It has been waiting for a very long time.
events.arc: The Chess Stones of Mount Song

effects.log: It is a masterpiece. Both sides are winning. You stay three days and cannot see the next move.
You lay a white stone. The mountain is silent. Something in your qi shifts, as if you have answered a question.
Some games are not for the living. You climb down with the board in your mind.

events.text: You return to the stone board on Mount Song. Someone has played a black stone in reply. There are no footprints in the snow but yours.
events.arc: The Chess Stones of Mount Song

effects.log: You play. You come back each winter and find a reply each time. The game is the best you have ever played.

choices.text: Wait in hiding for the other player

ok.log: At midnight the wind moves a pebble. You watch it roll into place, and do not quite believe what you saw.

fail.log: You fall asleep in the snow. In the morning a black stone has been played, and your cloak has been tucked around you.

events.text: Years into the game on Mount Song, the board is nearly full. Your next move will decide it. You realise that you have been playing against the mountain, or the wind, or someone dead, or yourself, and that it does not matter which.
events.arc: The Chess Stones of Mount Song

effects.log: You win by half a stone. The mountain does not mind. You walk down feeling lighter than you have in years.

choices.text: Play the move that makes it a draw

effects.log: A draw. All the stones lie in perfect balance. Snow starts to fall, and you laugh out loud.

choices.text: Leave the last move for whoever comes next

effects.log: You leave a single empty point and climb down. Someone else should have the pleasure.

events.text: On a lake south of the river, girls in round wooden tubs paddle through the lotus picking seed pods and singing a song that goes round and round. One tub has sprung a leak and is sinking very slowly, with its girl still singing in it.

choices.text: Wade out and push it to shore

effects.log: You get soaked to the chest. She keeps singing the whole time, and adds a verse about you.
Your throw lands perfectly on her head. She grabs it, laughing, and you haul her in.
The other tubs converge like ducks. Nobody needed you, but they wave.

events.text: The lotus girls remember you. They teach you their round-and-round song, and how to tell a ripe seed pod by the sound it makes when you flick it. They say they are going to sing at the Dragon Boat races this year.

effects.log: You learn all forty verses. One of them is about a fool who threw a rope at someone's head.

choices.text: Pick seeds with them for a day

effects.log: You eat as many as you pick. Your fingers are green for a week.

events.text: At the Dragon Boat races, the lotus girls sing from the bank, and the boat they are cheering for is losing badly. Its drummer has dropped his drumsticks into the lake.

choices.text: Drum the song on the gunwale for them

effects.log: You leap aboard and beat out the round-and-round song. The rowers find the rhythm. They win by a nose.
The whole bank takes up the song. The boat comes third, which for that village is a triumph.

events.text: A silk farm outside Suzhou has been abandoned because, the villagers say, the silkworms whisper. You spend a night in the long dark worm house, lying among the trays, and the whispering is real: a million tiny mouths eating mulberry leaves.

effects.log: It is the most soothing sound you have ever heard. You sleep like a stone.

choices.text: Look for who still feeds them

effects.log: Someone has been leaving fresh leaves. The footprints are very small.
You leave. The whispering follows you a little way, then lets you go.

events.text: The small footprints in the worm house belong to a girl of ten whose family fled the farm. She sneaks back every night to feed the worms, because nobody else would and they would die.

effects.log: You carry baskets of mulberry leaves together for a month. The worms spin. The cocoons are gold.

choices.text: Tell her family the truth about the whispering

effects.log: They come back, embarrassed, and stand in the worm house listening. Her father starts to laugh.

events.text: The silk farm is working again. The girl who fed the worms has grown, and she weaves a length of silk from that first golden harvest and gives it to you, wrapped in a mulberry leaf.

effects.log: It is so fine that people stop you in the street to ask where you got it. You tell them about the whispering.

choices.text: Sell it to fund her weaving school

effects.log: The silk fetches a fortune, and every coin goes to her school. She weeps and then bosses you about.

events.text: In a water town of Jiangnan there is an old stone bridge that, people say, shows twenty-four moons on the night of mid-autumn: one in the sky and twenty-three in the canals below. A poet has been sitting on it for a week trying to count them.

effects.log: You count nineteen. The poet counts twenty-two. You argue happily until dawn.
"Because the architect was in love," says the poet. "Everything absurd is built by someone in love."

choices.text: Buy the poet a bowl of noodles

effects.log: The poet eats like a wolf and dedicates a line to you.

events.text: On mid-autumn night you return to the bridge with the poet. The moon rises. You realise the moons are not in the canals but in the arches: each one is a perfect half-circle that the water completes, and the architect built them to catch the moon at different hours.

effects.log: You watch the moon walk under the bridge arch by arch all night. Twenty-four. Exactly.
The poet writes a poem that night that will be sung for a hundred years. Your name is in the second line.

events.text: A magistrate has ordered the old moon bridge pulled down for a wider, flatter one for carts. The whole water town is gathered, and the poet stands on the bridge with arms folded.

choices.text: Plead for the bridge before the magistrate

ok.log: You describe the twenty-four moons. The magistrate goes to see on mid-autumn night, and the order is torn up.

fail.log: The magistrate is unmoved, but the poet's poem moves the governor, and the bridge stays anyway.

choices.text: Stand on the bridge beside the poet

effects.log: You stand there for three days. The whole town brings food. In the end the cart road is built round the other side.

events.text: On the terraced hills of Longjing, the tea pickers say the best leaves grow on a single ancient bush at the top that nobody may pick but the oldest woman in the valley. She is ninety-four and climbs up there every spring.

effects.log: She climbs faster than you. At the top she picks nine leaves and gives you one to chew. It tastes like rain.
She lets you, then complains about how you carry it the whole way up.

choices.text: Pick tea on the lower terraces

effects.log: You earn a few coins and very green fingers.

events.text: The old tea picker is too ill to climb this spring. She asks you to go up to the ancient bush in her place and pick the nine leaves, and to sing to the bush while you do it, because it is used to her voice.

effects.log: You sing the only song you know. The bush does not seem to mind. You pick nine leaves.

ok.log: She croaks it to you from her bed. You sing it on the hill, and it sounds almost right.

fail.log: You forget the second verse and hum. The leaves are a little bitter.

events.text: You bring the nine leaves to the old tea picker. She brews them in a cracked cup, drinks, and smiles. "You sang badly," she says. "Good. The bush needs a new voice. Go up every spring."

choices.text: Promise to go up every spring

effects.log: You do, for as long as you can. The valley starts calling the bush by your name.

choices.text: Find a young picker to take it on

effects.log: You find a shy boy who sings like a lark. The old woman approves of him at once, and of you for finding him.

events.text: At dusk on the Li River, an old fisherman poles a bamboo raft with six cormorants perched on it, each with a ring round its throat. He says his birds can catch more fish than any martial artist alive. He offers you a contest, the loser cooks.

ok.log: You snatch eleven fish. The cormorants catch thirty. You cook, and he praises your hands.

fail.log: You fall in the river. The cormorants seem to laugh. You cook.

effects.log: You cook. He eats, and tells you the names of all six birds.
He shrugs and poles away into the dusk, the birds bobbing.

events.text: The old cormorant fisherman is ill, and his birds will not fish for anyone else. He asks you to try, since you cooked for them once and they remember the smell of you.

ok.log: The birds watch you a long time, then dive. You bring back a full basket.

fail.log: The birds sit and stare at you all evening. You catch one fish yourself and they look embarrassed for you.

choices.text: Fish for him with a net instead

effects.log: You bring him fish every day until he is well. The birds sulk the whole time.

events.text: The old cormorant fisherman has died, and his six birds sit on the empty raft, refusing food. His granddaughter wants to learn to fish with them, but they will not dive for her.

choices.text: Show her what the old man did

effects.log: You remember his whistle and the slap of the pole. The birds dive for her at last.
You take the rings off their throats. Five fly off. One stays, and fishes for her for love.

events.text: A retired minister's garden in Suzhou is famous for its rockeries, and for the fact that guests get lost in it for hours. You go in at noon. At dusk you are still in it, and you have passed the same moon gate four times.

ok.log: It is a formation, made of rocks and water. Once you see it, you walk out in ten steps.

fail.log: A servant finds you at midnight and leads you out, kindly, by the sleeve.

effects.log: You sit by a pond and watch the carp. When you stop trying, you find the way out at once.

events.text: The minister who built the maze garden invites you back. He was an array master in his youth, he admits, and he has hidden a final room in the garden that nobody has ever found. He wants to know if you can.

ok.log: Behind a waterfall of rocks, a tiny pavilion with a single cup of tea, still warm. He applauds.

fail.log: You find a cupboard full of brooms. He applauds anyway.

effects.log: "Then it would not be hidden," he says, delighted, and gives you a book on rockeries instead.

events.text: The old minister is dying, and asks you to his garden. He wants you to be the keeper of the hidden pavilion: to bring one person there every ten years who has earned it, and pour them the tea.

effects.log: He gives you the key, which is not a key but a way of walking. You will never forget it.
The gardener has known all along. The minister laughs until he coughs. "Of course he has."

events.text: The paddies are flooding after a week of rain, and a farmer is wading through them with a lantern, calling for something. He says his family's rice spirit has been washed out of its little shrine on the dyke.

choices.text: Help him search the flooded fields

effects.log: You find a small clay figure stuck in the mud, smiling. The farmer hugs it and then you.
You pile stones all night. The flood stops rising. In the morning the clay figure is sitting on top of your stones.

choices.text: Tell him it is just clay

effects.log: He looks at you with great pity and keeps searching.

events.text: Since you saved the rice spirit, the farmer's paddies have yielded double. He insists the spirit likes you. He wants you to carry it to its "home", a temple a hundred li away, so it can be blessed.

effects.log: It is heavier with every li. At the temple the monk says it has not been brought in two hundred years.
The farmer goes himself. When he returns, the spirit is wearing a tiny new robe.

events.text: The monk at the rice temple sends a message: every village in the valley has brought its rice spirit to be blessed, the first time in centuries, and they are holding a festival. You are to lead the procession.

effects.log: You walk at the front carrying the little clay figure while ten thousand farmers sing. It is ridiculous and wonderful.

choices.text: Walk at the back with the farmer

effects.log: You walk at the back. Nobody notices you. It is the best festival of your life.

events.text: In a hut by a lake an old painter has painted the same mountain every day for sixty years. The walls are papered with mountains. He says he has not yet got it right, and will know it when he does, because the mountain will nod.

effects.log: Your qi slows to the rhythm of his brush. By evening you see the mountain differently.
You paint a lumpy mountain. He studies it for a long time and says it is honest.
You leave. Behind you he starts painting again, with a soft sound like rain.

events.text: You return to the painter of one mountain. He has stopped painting. He has, he says, finally got it right, and the mountain nodded. He is now afraid to paint anything else.

effects.log: It is four brush strokes. You look at it and feel the mountain lean towards you. Your knees are weak.
"Paint the lake," you say. He looks at it as if it were a dragon. Then he dips his brush.

events.text: The old painter has died, and left you the four-stroke painting. Collectors offer you fortunes. The mountain stands across the lake as it always has.

effects.log: You hang it where you meditate. On hard days the mountain still leans close.

choices.text: Give it to the lake village

effects.log: They hang it in the village hall. Children grow up looking at it. Some of them paint.
You are rich, briefly. The collector never once looks at the real mountain.

events.text: In the bamboo forests above a small temple, a black-and-white bear sits in the path eating bamboo, and will not move. Behind it a young monk is waiting very patiently with a basket of shoots for the temple kitchen.
events.arc: The Monk and the Bamboo Bear

effects.log: You wait. The bear eats. Two hours later it rolls over and goes to sleep in the path. The monk sighs and sits down.
It takes the shoot, delicately, and then the whole basket. The monk looks at you.

ok.log: You push. The bear does not notice. You push harder. It moves one step, out of politeness.

fail.log: It sits on you briefly. You lose interest in moving bears.

events.text: The young monk and the bamboo bear have reached an arrangement: he brings it the woody old shoots, it lets him pass with the tender ones. He wants to show you something the bear showed him, higher up the mountain.
events.arc: The Monk and the Bamboo Bear

effects.log: The bear leads you both to a spring nobody knew of, cold and sweet, under a stand of purple bamboo.

choices.text: Ask how a bear showed him anything

effects.log: "It walked ahead and looked back," he says. "That is what all teachers do."

events.text: You come back to the purple-bamboo spring years later. The young monk is the temple's abbot now. The bear is very old and sleeps by the spring all day. The abbot has built a little roof over it.
events.arc: The Monk and the Bamboo Bear

effects.log: The old bear opens one eye and takes one shoot, delicately. The abbot laughs.

choices.text: Sit by the spring and meditate

effects.log: The water, the bamboo, the bear breathing. Your qi settles like silt in still water.

events.text: At the golden summit of Mount Emei, pilgrims wait on the cliff edge for the Buddha's Light: a halo of rainbow that sometimes rings your own shadow on the sea of clouds below. You wait a whole afternoon, and the clouds stay grey.

effects.log: An old woman says she has come twelve times and seen it once, and that once was worth all the others.
The cold is bitter. The stars over the clouds are like spilled rice.
You go down. At the bottom you learn it appeared an hour after you left.

events.text: You climb Emei again. This time, as the sun drops, the clouds part below the cliff, and your shadow appears on them with a circle of rainbow round its head. It moves when you move.

effects.log: It raises a hand to you. Something in you that has been clenched for years lets go.
The halo fades as you step back. You are glad you saw it, and glad you did not step forward.

events.text: The old pilgrim woman from Emei is at the summit again, now too frail to walk, carried in a chair by her grandsons. She asks you to stay with her, in case it comes.

effects.log: It comes. She laughs out loud and grips your hand. Two halos, side by side.

choices.text: Carry her chair yourself next time

effects.log: You carry her up three more springs. She sees it twice more.

events.text: In a Chengdu market, a cook with arms like hams challenges all passers-by to eat a bowl of his "Nine Hells" noodles without drinking water. Nobody has ever finished. The prize is a lifetime of free noodles.

ok.log: You finish, sweating fire. The market cheers. The cook looks at you with new respect and some fear.

fail.log: You make it three bites. Your qi rebels. You drink a whole bucket of water to great applause.

effects.log: A monk, a soldier and a scholar all fail magnificently. You laugh until you hurt.

events.text: The pepper cook has heard of a rival in Chongqing who claims his own noodles are hotter. He wants you, his champion, to go and eat the rival's bowl, for the honour of Chengdu.

ok.log: You finish it. The Chongqing cook bows to you, weeping, though possibly from the fumes.

fail.log: You finish it but cannot speak for a week. Chengdu claims victory anyway.

effects.log: They meet. They argue about pepper for nine hours and become best friends.

events.text: The two pepper cooks have opened a restaurant together, halfway between their cities. On the wall is a painting of you with flames coming out of your ears. Your lifetime of free noodles now includes both menus.

choices.text: Eat there as often as you can

effects.log: Your constitution grows remarkable. Poisons have trouble with you now.

choices.text: Ask them to take down the painting

effects.log: They refuse, and add a second one.

events.text: Deep in the Sichuan hills, a garden wall has a sign: "Every plant inside will kill you. Welcome." The gate is open. A very old gardener inside is pruning something purple with tongs.

choices.text: Ask if you may come in

effects.log: "Touch nothing," the gardener says. You walk the paths with your hands behind your back for an hour.

ok.log: You name it. The gardener stops pruning and looks at you properly for the first time.

fail.log: You name it wrongly. "That one would have killed you more slowly," the gardener says.

choices.text: Read the sign twice and walk on

effects.log: Some welcomes are better refused. You walk on.

events.text: The poison gardener asks you a riddle: in this garden, every plant kills, and every plant also cures something. Which cures the gardener's own illness, a cough that has lasted twenty years?

ok.log: The grey moss by the well. The gardener laughs and coughs and says it was too obvious to see.

fail.log: You pick wrong, but the gardener is delighted: that one cures something else, which nobody knew.

effects.log: "Good," the gardener says. "Nobody who knows walks out of this garden."

events.text: The poison gardener's cough has gone for the first time in twenty years. The gardener gives you a cutting of grey moss in a sealed pot and a small book of the garden's cures, written in a cramped hand.

effects.log: Every page is a poison and its cure. You read it twice and never think of a plant the same way again.

choices.text: Give the moss to a village doctor

effects.log: A whole valley with a cough that never ends breathes easily that winter.

events.text: The old plank road into Shu hangs from a cliff on wooden beams driven into the rock, a thousand feet above a river. Halfway across, a mule has stopped and refuses to go on, and behind it a queue of furious travellers is growing.

effects.log: You talk nonsense to it in a soft voice for an hour. It walks on. The queue cheers.

ok.log: You shoulder its packs. Lightened, it trots across. You arrive with very sore shoulders.

fail.log: The packs are heavier than they look. You drop one. It is only blankets, thankfully.

choices.text: Go round by the long road

effects.log: Three extra days. You see some fine waterfalls.

events.text: The mule's owner on the plank road was a salt merchant, and has not forgotten you. Now a beam on the road has rotted and fallen, and the merchant has a cart of salt stuck on one side and a town without salt on the other.

choices.text: Leap the gap with the sacks

ok.log: You cross twenty times with a sack on your back, a thousand feet above the river. The town gets its salt.

fail.log: You make three crossings before your nerve fails. It is enough, just.

choices.text: Help the road crew drive a new beam

effects.log: It takes four days and every curse you know. The new beam is very good.

events.text: The town at the end of the plank road has carved a new beam with your name burned into it and set it into the cliff. Whenever you cross, the toll keeper waves you through for nothing and tells everyone about the salt.

choices.text: Walk the road again for the view

effects.log: You stop on your own beam and look down at the river, very small, and do not feel afraid.
The toll keeper refuses. You leave the coins on the beam. They are gone by morning.

events.text: You walk into a mist in the Sichuan hills and out of it into a village where everyone wears clothes of a dynasty that ended four hundred years ago. They are not ghosts; they are farming. They are very surprised by your shoes.

effects.log: They feed you millet and ask about the emperor. You do not have the heart to tell them which one.
"We walked into the mist to escape a war," an elder says. "Is it over?"

choices.text: Walk back into the mist at once

effects.log: You come out on the ordinary road with your heart pounding. The mist is gone.

events.text: You find the mist again after a long search. In the hidden village no time seems to have passed: the same elder, the same millet. They ask if the war is over now.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: it ended long ago

effects.log: The elder is quiet. Then says: "Then perhaps we can leave." Half the village looks afraid; half looks at the mist.

choices.text: Say nothing, and stay a season

effects.log: You live a season out of time. When you leave, your hair has not grown at all.

events.text: Some of the mist village have walked out with you into the world, blinking, holding their old coins. The others stayed. The mist has thinned to almost nothing, and you are not sure it will come back.

effects.log: You find them land and teach them about money. They teach a town how to grow millet in a way nobody remembered.

choices.text: Walk back into the last of the mist

effects.log: You say goodbye to those who stayed. The mist closes behind you, gently, and is gone.

events.text: At Zigong they drill salt wells a thousand feet deep with bamboo pipes, and the brine comes up with a gas that burns. An old driller lowers a lantern down an abandoned well and swears he hears singing at the bottom.

effects.log: It is wind in the pipes, you think. Mostly. It does sound like singing.

choices.text: Lower yourself on the rope a little

effects.log: Twenty feet down the singing is louder and the air smells of eggs. You climb out fast.

choices.text: Help at a working well instead

effects.log: You haul brine for a day and earn your supper.

events.text: The old driller has worked it out: the abandoned well sings before the gas comes up, the way birds go quiet before an earthquake. Today it is singing very loudly, and a crew is working at the well next to it.

effects.log: They drop their tools and run. Behind them the next well spits fire. Nobody is hurt.

ok.log: You heave the stone cap over it. The singing stops. The gas goes elsewhere, harmlessly.

fail.log: The cap slips. A gust of foul gas sends you staggering, but the crew hears the noise and runs.

events.text: The salt workers of Zigong have hung a bamboo pipe at the mouth of every well, and taught their children to listen to it. They call it your bell. The old driller has retired and spends his days telling the story wrongly.

effects.log: He refuses to be corrected. In his version you fight a fire dragon. You decide you like it.

choices.text: Teach the children to listen properly

effects.log: You spend a week with them at the wells. They can hear the gas coming better than you can now.

events.text: On a boat through the Three Gorges, the cliffs are so high the sky is a blue thread. Monkeys scream from the rocks, and one drops onto the deck, snatches your bag, and climbs the mast with it.
events.arc: The Monkeys of the Three Gorges

ok.log: You reach the top. The monkey hands back your bag, impressed, minus one bun.

fail.log: You climb halfway. The monkey throws your bag into the river and screams with laughter.

choices.text: Offer it a bun in exchange

effects.log: The monkey considers. It takes the bun, keeps the bag, and leaves you a smooth green stone.
Eventually it gets bored and drops the bag on the boatman's head.

events.text: Back in the Gorges, the boatman points: the green stone the monkey left you is the same stone as the old shrine on the cliff, a carved face so worn it is almost gone. The monkeys, he says, have been stealing pieces of it for a century.
events.arc: The Monkeys of the Three Gorges

choices.text: Return the stone to the shrine

effects.log: You climb the cliff and press it into the empty socket of an eye. The monkeys go silent all along the gorge.
It is warm in your hand. You decide the monkeys gave it to you on purpose.

events.text: You sail the Three Gorges again. The monkeys, who once robbed every boat, now line the cliffs and watch. One drops onto the deck, very carefully, and leaves a peach at your feet.
events.arc: The Monkeys of the Three Gorges

effects.log: It is the sweetest peach of your life. The monkeys scream approval.

choices.text: Bow to the shrine as you pass

effects.log: The worn face on the cliff seems, today, to have two eyes.

events.text: On a crumbling stretch of the old Wall, one beacon tower still has smoke coming from it. Inside, an old soldier is tending a fire. Nobody has relieved him, he says, for thirty-one years, and he cannot leave his post without orders.

choices.text: Share his fire for the night

effects.log: He tells you about every raid he ever saw, and about the wolf that comes to the tower every winter.
You haul a sack of millet and some salt up the hill. He salutes you gravely.

choices.text: Tell him the garrison is gone

effects.log: "Then I am the garrison," he says, and goes back to his fire.

events.text: You return to the beacon tower on the Wall. The old soldier is coughing badly. He asks you, as the only other person he has spoken to in years, whether you think his orders still stand.

ok.log: In a fort's archive you find an order relieving his whole unit, dated thirty years ago. It never reached him.

fail.log: The records are ash. You write him an order yourself, as kindly as you can.

choices.text: Stay and keep the fire while he rests

effects.log: You keep the beacon for a month. He sleeps for most of it, smiling.

events.text: The old soldier of the beacon tower reads his relief order three times. Then he puts out the fire for the first time in thirty-one years, folds his old banner, and asks you which way the nearest village is.

effects.log: The village takes him in. The children follow him everywhere. He teaches them to march, very badly.

choices.text: Light the beacon one last time for him

effects.log: It burns all night. Along the Wall, three other towers you thought were dead answer with fire.

events.text: On the northern grasslands you meet a herder girl of fourteen with a golden eagle on her arm, nearly as big as she is. Her father says girls cannot hunt with eagles. The eagle seems to disagree with him.

effects.log: The eagle drops like a stone and takes a fox in the grass. The girl whoops. Her father pretends not to watch.

ok.log: It steps onto your arm and stares through you. It weighs as much as a child.

fail.log: It bites your glove off. The girl laughs so hard she sits down.

effects.log: You ride on through the grass. Behind you an eagle screams.

events.text: The herders are holding an eagle festival, and the eagle girl wants to fly her bird in the contest. Her father refuses to let her enter, and the elders agree with him.

choices.text: Speak to the elders for her

ok.log: You argue for an hour. An old grandmother finally says she flew an eagle herself once. The girl enters.

fail.log: The elders refuse. The girl enters anyway, in her brother's coat.

effects.log: You stay out of it. That night her eagle steals the elders' supper off the fire.

events.text: At the eagle festival the herder girl's bird takes the prize: it dives from so high it is only a speck, and comes up carrying the lure before anyone sees it move. Her father is shouting louder than anybody.

effects.log: He grabs you round the shoulders, shouting. He gives you a horse. You sell it to a herder who needs it more, for a good price.
She teaches you a winter. You learn more about patience from her eagle than from any master.

events.text: When the northern river freezes a yard thick, a market appears on the ice: horses, furs, iron pots, roasted mutton, people from both banks who are at war in summer and trade in winter. You wander it with your breath steaming.

effects.log: The hat is enormous and smells of goat. It is the warmest thing you will ever own.
Two men wrestle on the ice, slipping, laughing, falling. You join in and fall too.

choices.text: Ask why the war stops in winter

effects.log: "The river is a road in winter," an old trader says. "Nobody burns a road."

events.text: At the ice market again, the wrestlers remember you. The champion, a vast herder named Batu, wants a proper match before the thaw. Half the market gathers on the ice.

ok.log: You throw him. He lies on the ice laughing, then lifts you over his head. You are now his sworn sibling, apparently.

fail.log: He throws you nine yards across the ice. You slide into a pot seller. Everyone cheers.

choices.text: Challenge him to a race on the ice instead

effects.log: You both fall over at the first step. It is declared a draw.

events.text: This winter the ice is thin, and the river market is cancelled. On the far bank you can see Batu, waving his arms. Between you, black water shows through the ice.

choices.text: Shout across and promise next year

effects.log: He bellows something cheerful back. Next winter the ice is thick and he crushes you in a hug.

ok.log: You run across the cracking ice. Batu catches you. Both banks applaud.

fail.log: You go through up to the waist. Batu drags you out and wraps you in his coat, roaring.

events.text: A fort on the frontier was abandoned after a lost battle a century ago. Shepherds say that on moonless nights, the gates open and a ghostly garrison drills in the courtyard. You camp outside it on a moonless night.

effects.log: They are there. Pale, silent, drilling a spear form you have never seen, over and over.
They do not see you. One of them is very young and keeps getting the form wrong.
You leave. The shepherds call you sensible, and you are.

events.text: You come back to the ghost garrison and learn the spear form by watching it. On the third night, the young ghost who always got it wrong stops, turns, and looks straight at you.

effects.log: You go through it step by step. He follows. On the last step, he gets it right, and smiles.

ok.log: You drill all night beside the dead. At dawn the form is part of your body.

fail.log: Your arms give out before the ghosts do. They wait politely while you rest.

events.text: On the next moonless night, the ghost garrison does not drill. They stand in ranks at the open gate, the young one at the front, and their captain bows to you. Then they march out of the fort and into the dark grass, and do not come back.

effects.log: The steppe is silent. In the morning the gates have fallen shut by themselves.

choices.text: Bury their old spears in the courtyard

effects.log: You find them rusting in the barracks and bury them under a stone. You feel watched, kindly.

events.text: In a blizzard on the northern steppe you shelter in a shepherd's empty hut, and find you are sharing it with a grey wolf with an arrow in its leg. It shows its teeth and does not move. Neither of you can leave.

effects.log: It snaps at your sleeve but not at you. The arrow comes free. It sleeps against the far wall all night.
It eats without taking its eyes off you. At dawn it is gone, and so is the rest of your meat.

ok.log: You drive it into the snow. It looks back once. You do not sleep well.

fail.log: It drives you into the corner instead. You spend the night very still.

events.text: Lost again in a northern snowstorm, you are near the end of your strength when a grey wolf limps out of the white, looks at you, and walks on ahead, stopping every few steps.

effects.log: It leads you to a herders' camp and sits on a ridge watching until they take you in. Then it is gone.

choices.text: Dig in and wait out the storm

effects.log: You dig a snow cave. At dawn there are wolf tracks circling it, as if something stood guard all night.

events.text: The herders who took you in say the limping grey wolf has a den in the rocks above their winter camp, and has never once taken one of their sheep. Now there are cubs. Hunters from the town want the pelts.

effects.log: You stand on the path to the rocks for three days. The hunters decide there are easier wolves.

choices.text: Lead the hunters off on a false trail

ok.log: You lead them a week into the wrong mountains. They come home with nothing and a cold each.

fail.log: They see through it, but by then the wolf has moved her cubs. You never see them again, which is how it should be.

events.text: The herders of the far north speak of a white stallion that runs with the wind and has never been ridden. At dawn on a frost-white plain you see it: a horse of no colour at all, watching you from a hill, as still as a carving.

effects.log: It lets you come within fifty paces, then is suddenly a mile away without seeming to run.
You sit all day. It grazes nearer and nearer. At dusk it is close enough to hear it breathe.

ok.log: You run with all your qi. For a moment you run beside it. Then it is gone, and you are laughing.

fail.log: It does not even bother to run. You fall in the frost.

events.text: You return to the frost plain every dawn for a month. On the last morning the white stallion walks straight to you and stands, waiting.

ok.log: It runs. The steppe goes by like a river. You ride until noon and then it stops and you slide off, dizzy.

fail.log: It throws you, very gently, into a snowdrift. It stays and lets you try again tomorrow.

effects.log: It is warm, warmer than any horse. It leans into your hand for a breath, then walks away.

events.text: A khan's horse catchers have come for the white stallion with lassos and a hundred riders, to give it to their lord. They have it penned in a ravine, and it is screaming.

ok.log: You scatter them. The white horse goes past you like a wind and stops once on the ridge to look back.

fail.log: They beat you back, but in the confusion the horse leaps the ravine wall and is gone.

choices.text: Cut the ropes in the night

effects.log: You slip in at midnight. The horse makes no sound as you cut it free. By dawn there are only its tracks, and then not even those.

events.text: On the frontier there is a field where the grass grows thin, because the ground is half arrowheads from a battle so old nobody remembers who fought it. Children collect them and sell them to travellers in the town.

effects.log: The child charges you double and tells you a battle story that is clearly invented on the spot.
You walk until sunset. The arrowheads crunch like gravel. It is very quiet.

choices.text: Pick up an arrowhead and study it

effects.log: It is beautifully made. Somebody took great care with this, a thousand years ago.

events.text: Walking the arrowhead field again, you find among the bronze heads something else: a jade seal, half buried. On it is the name of a general who, the histories say, deserted. The seal is lying at the very front of the battle line.

choices.text: Take the seal to the town scholar

effects.log: He reads it, and reads the histories, and goes very pale. The general did not desert. He was first to fall.

choices.text: Bury it again where it lay

effects.log: You put it back. Some truths have waited long enough to wait a little more.

events.text: The town scholar has written to the capital about the jade seal and the general who did not desert. A reply comes: the general's descendants, who have lived in disgrace for a thousand years, are coming to see the field.

effects.log: An old woman finds the spot where the seal lay, and kneels, and does not get up for an hour.
The children tell the true story now, with only small inventions. The descendants pay them double.

events.text: In a herders' camp on the grass sea, an old blind storyteller sings an epic that takes, they say, nine nights to finish. You arrive on the fourth night, in the middle of a battle between a hero and a sky giant.
events.arc: The Storyteller of the Grass Sea

choices.text: Stay for all five remaining nights

effects.log: You hear the whole end. On the ninth night the hero comes home, old, and his horse knows him.
Nobody will tell you. "Come back next year," they say. "He starts it again in autumn."
The sky giant is still winning when you leave. You think about it for weeks.

events.text: You come back to the herders' camp in autumn to hear the storyteller's epic from the beginning. He has a cough now, and says this may be the last time. No one in the camp knows the whole song.
events.arc: The Storyteller of the Grass Sea

ok.log: Nine nights, nine days of practice. You can sing it, roughly. He corrects every line, delighted.

fail.log: You learn six nights of it. He says six is more than anyone else has.

choices.text: Find a child in the camp to learn it

effects.log: A girl with a memory like a trap learns it all. You only learn the part with the horse.

events.text: The blind storyteller has died. This autumn, the camp gathers in the big yurt and turns to you, because you are the one who learned his song.
events.arc: The Storyteller of the Grass Sea

effects.log: You stumble on the first night. By the fifth the song carries you. On the ninth the horse knows the hero, and the whole yurt weeps.

choices.text: Sing the first night and teach the rest

effects.log: You sing one night and teach a dozen young herders the rest. The song goes on.

events.text: On a rocky island off the coast, the pearl divers are all women, and the best of them is seventy-eight. She holds her breath longer than anyone, and laughs at anyone who tries to match her. Today she points at you.

ok.log: You come up gasping after a minute. She comes up after three, with an oyster, and pats your head.

fail.log: You come up after twenty heartbeats, coughing seawater. The whole beach applauds anyway.

choices.text: Mind the baskets on the shore

effects.log: You guard the baskets from gulls all day. It is harder than diving.
She calls you a land crab, fondly.

events.text: The old pearl diver teaches you to breathe the way the island women do: slow, deep, down into the belly, so the sea cannot find the bottom of you. She says it is the same as any qi method, only wetter.

effects.log: After a month you can stay under two minutes. Your qi feels like a tide, deep and slow.
She shows you a black pearl on a string round her neck and will not say where she found it.

events.text: The old pearl diver is too stiff to dive this year. She sends you down instead, to an underwater rock shaped like a sleeping dog, where, she says, the oysters are oldest.

ok.log: You come up after a long time with an oyster as big as a plate. Inside it is a pearl like a small moon.

fail.log: You touch the rock and must come up. She laughs and says you were close, which is a kind lie.

choices.text: Bring her to the beach to watch

effects.log: You carry her to the rocks on your back. She shouts instructions all day and is happy.

events.text: At the end of a cape called Turtle Head, an old stone tower burns a fire every night to warn ships off the rocks. Its keeper has broken a leg. Tonight a storm is coming, and the fire must be kept.

effects.log: You haul wood up a hundred steps all night in the wind. At dawn three fishing junks come home safely.
You run to the village through the rain. They come with wood, and the fire never falters.
You set the bone. He curses you all the way through, then thanks you.

events.text: On another stormy night you are back at the Turtle Head lighthouse. A ship that is not a fishing junk is coming in too close: a pirate ship, the keeper says, that wants the fire put out so the merchant ship behind it will wreck.

choices.text: Hold the tower against the pirates

ok.log: They come up the steps and you throw them down again. The fire burns. The merchant ship sails past safely.

fail.log: You are driven back to the top of the tower, but the fire is still burning when they give up.

effects.log: You throw on everything: furniture, rope, the keeper's chair. The fire roars. Both ships turn away from the rocks.

events.text: The merchant ship you saved at Turtle Head was carrying rice to a starving province. The provincial governor has sent money to rebuild the lighthouse in stone and brass, and a plaque with your name on it.

choices.text: Help the keeper with the new tower

effects.log: The new fire is a lamp with a brass mirror. It shines twenty li out to sea.

choices.text: Give your plaque to the keeper

effects.log: He hangs it inside, facing the wall, and says it is better that way. You agree.

events.text: A strange ship has anchored in the harbour: three masts, square sails, and sailors with hair the colour of straw. Nobody can understand them, and the harbour master has sent for soldiers.
events.arc: The Ship From Beyond the Sea

effects.log: After an hour of waving, you have learned their word for water and taught them yours for noodle.
You row out with a pot of rice. They eat as if starving, which, it turns out, they are.
The soldiers arrive. Nobody does anything for a day. Then everyone goes home.

events.text: The foreign sailors have been allowed to stay while their ship is repaired. Their ship's doctor, a tall woman with a box of strange instruments, wants to trade knowledge with someone who knows Chinese medicine.
events.arc: The Ship From Beyond the Sea

ok.log: You show her acupuncture; she shows you a glass that makes small things large. You both stare at a drop of pond water, amazed.

fail.log: You understand one word in ten. But you both laugh at the same moments, which is something.

choices.text: Show her the harbour market instead

effects.log: She buys everything that smells strange. You carry it all.

events.text: The foreign ship is repaired and sails at dawn. The ship's doctor gives you a small glass lens wrapped in cloth and a drawing of her country, which seems to be very cold.
events.arc: The Ship From Beyond the Sea

choices.text: Use the lens to study herbs

effects.log: Through it, every leaf is a landscape. Your medicine improves in ways your teachers cannot explain.

choices.text: Give her a tea brick in return

effects.log: She bows like a local. The ship sails. You never learn if it got home.

events.text: After a great typhoon, a new island has appeared off the coast: a long hump of black sand and broken coral, steaming in the sun. Fishermen are afraid of it. Nobody has set foot on it.

effects.log: You are the first person ever to stand on it. The sand is warm. Crabs watch you.

choices.text: Ask the old fishermen about it

effects.log: "It comes up every hundred years," says the oldest, "and brings something with it."
In a month it is half gone already. Some places are not meant to stay.

events.text: On the typhoon island, half eaten by the sea, the waves have uncovered a ship's timbers in the black sand: a treasure junk of the old navy, sunk three hundred years ago and thrown up again.

ok.log: In the hold, in rotted chests, a fortune in old silver and a sealed jar of seeds.

fail.log: The sand slides back as fast as you dig. You get a handful of old coins.

effects.log: Inside, a logbook in perfect condition: a voyage to lands beyond the sea, and a map.

events.text: The typhoon island has sunk back under the waves, taking the old treasure junk with it. You rowed away with what you could carry, and the fishermen of the coast look at you as if you had come back from the dead.

choices.text: Share the find with the fishing village

effects.log: The village gets new boats and nets. They name the reef where the island sank after you.

choices.text: Plant the seeds from the wreck

effects.log: A jar of them was lodged in the timbers. They sprout into a tree nobody recognises, with fruit that tastes of cinnamon and rain.

choices.text: Keep the logbook and study the map

effects.log: You study it for years. It changes the way you look at the edge of the world.

events.text: Two fishing villages on the coast have been at war for three generations over a single rock in the bay, where the biggest crabs live. Today both villages are out on the rock with nets, shouting.

effects.log: Nobody knows. Both sides are certain the other side started it.
You count them. There are far more crabs than either village could ever eat.
Both villages chase you. It is the first thing they have ever done together.

events.text: The crab war has escalated: one village has painted their boats red, the other blue, and the children of the two villages are forbidden to speak. You notice that a red-boat boy and a blue-boat girl meet every evening on the crab rock anyway.

effects.log: They show you the best crab hole on the rock. It is enormous.
You and the two children cook up a plan involving a lot of crabs and both villages at once.

events.text: At the mid-autumn festival, the red-boat boy and the blue-boat girl light a huge fire on the crab rock and cook a feast of crabs, and invite both villages. Everyone comes, scowling, to see who dares.

effects.log: You cook all night. By midnight the two village heads are arguing about crab sauce, not the rock.

choices.text: Tell the story of the war, as you know it

effects.log: You tell them nobody remembers how it started. An old woman says she does: it was a stolen hat. Everyone laughs, at last.

events.text: A sea cave under the cliffs can only be entered at the lowest tide, and then only for an hour. Smugglers used it once. Now, the coast guards say, it is empty. There are fresh footprints in the sand at its mouth.

ok.log: You find casks of salt, stamped with the seal of the magistrate himself. Then the tide turns and you swim for it.

fail.log: The tide comes in early. You get out soaked and with nothing.

effects.log: At dusk a boat slides in with no lantern. You recognise the man at the oars: the magistrate's clerk.
The guards shrug. "Crabs," they say. Crabs with boots.

events.text: You have proof that the magistrate is smuggling salt through the sea cave and starving the poor of the coast by keeping the price high. The question is what to do with it.

choices.text: Take the proof to the provincial governor

ok.log: The governor reads it and turns red. The magistrate is gone within a month. Salt is cheap again.

fail.log: The governor is the magistrate's cousin. You are told politely to leave the province for a while.

choices.text: Give the salt away at night

effects.log: You empty the cave into every poor kitchen on the coast. The magistrate cannot complain without confessing.

events.text: The coast villages have a new song about the night salt fell from the sky. A small girl sings it to you on the road, not knowing who you are, and gets every detail wrong except the last line, which is that the poor ate well that winter.

choices.text: Sing the last line with her

effects.log: She is delighted that you know it. So are you.
She refuses the correction firmly, and you decide she is right.

events.text: On a far headland stands a temple to the Sea Mother, protector of sailors. The keeper is an old nun who says the goddess has stopped answering prayers this year, and the boats are not coming home.
events.arc: The Temple of the Sea Mother

choices.text: Pray in the temple all night

effects.log: You meditate until dawn. In the grey light you are sure, very sure, that something is listening.

choices.text: Ask the sailors what they have seen

effects.log: They speak of a great dark shape under the water, moving against the current.

choices.text: Offer silver for the temple roof

effects.log: The nun thanks you. The roof does not leak. The boats still do not come home.

events.text: Out on the open sea in a fisherman's boat, you see the dark shape under the water: a whale, an immense old one, tangled in a net of a thousand broken lines from a thousand boats, dragging them off course. It is exhausted.
events.arc: The Temple of the Sea Mother

ok.log: You cut for an hour in the cold. The whale rolls one huge eye towards you and sinks into the deep, free.

fail.log: You cut half the nets. The whale breaks the rest itself, nearly drowning you, and is gone.

choices.text: Bring the whole fleet to free it

effects.log: Fifty boats with knives. It takes all day. When it is done the whale sings, and every sailor weeps.

events.text: The boats are coming home again. The old nun of the Sea Mother's temple says the goddess has answered at last, and she asks you to carve the story into the temple wall.
events.arc: The Temple of the Sea Mother

effects.log: You carve it badly but with great love. Sailors touch it for luck as they pass.

choices.text: Carve the sailors with their knives

effects.log: You carve the fleet, and the sailors find their own faces. They bring their children to see.

events.text: At a spring kite festival on the beach, a child's paper kite, shaped like a carp, goes up and up and simply will not come down. It has been up for three days. People have started to bow to it.
events.arc: The Kite That Would Not Come Down

choices.text: Climb the cliff and catch the line

ok.log: You catch the line. It pulls like a living thing. You hand it back to the child, who refuses to take it.

fail.log: You slip and slide down the cliff on your back. The kite stays up.

choices.text: Ask the child where it came from

effects.log: "My grandfather made it before he died," the child says. "He said it would find him."

choices.text: Fly your own kite beside it

effects.log: You fly a cheap paper dragon beside it for an afternoon. It is the most peaceful day you can remember.

events.text: The carp kite is still up after a month. You go back to the beach with the child, and the line in your hands goes slack for the first time. The kite comes down slowly, slowly, and lands in the child's arms.
events.arc: The Kite That Would Not Come Down

effects.log: On the inside, in tiny brush strokes, the grandfather has written a letter to the child. You turn away to let them read it.

choices.text: Help the child fly it again tomorrow

effects.log: It flies again, an ordinary kite now. It comes down when it is called.

events.text: The child of the carp kite has grown up and runs a kite shop on the beach. On the wall, in a glass frame, is the old carp, and beside it a new kite with your face painted on it, flying very badly.
events.arc: The Kite That Would Not Come Down

choices.text: Buy the kite with your face

effects.log: It flies as badly as the painting suggests. You fly it anyway, all afternoon, and laugh.

choices.text: Order a carp kite for a stranger's child

effects.log: You hand it to a crying child on the beach. It flies straight up and stays there. Of course it does.

events.text: Near Dunhuang there are dunes that sing: when you slide down them, the sand roars like a drum and a thousand voices. A camel driver bets you cannot slide all the way down the biggest one without stopping.

ok.log: You go down in a roar of sand like thunder. At the bottom you are laughing too hard to stand.

fail.log: You tumble most of the way. The dune sings anyway. Sand gets everywhere.

effects.log: You sit at the top and listen to other people slide. It sounds like an army underground.
The camel driver calls you a coward and gives you a dried apricot.

events.text: At night the singing dunes sing by themselves, the camel driver tells you, without anyone sliding. He has heard it twice in thirty years. Tonight the wind is very still, and he wakes you and puts a finger to his lips.

effects.log: Under the stars, the whole desert hums one long low note. You feel it in your teeth and in your qi.

choices.text: Climb the dune in the dark

effects.log: At the top the sound is everywhere and nowhere. You lie down in the sand and it hums through you.

events.text: The old camel driver is retiring from the desert roads. On his last night he asks you to slide the great dune with him, one last time, for luck.

effects.log: You go down side by side, roaring like a storm. At the bottom he weeps with laughter and gives you his camel bell.
He slides down shouting like a boy. At the bottom he lies in the sand and does not get up for a long time, smiling.

events.text: In the cliffs near the Silk Road, a hundred caves are painted floor to ceiling with Buddhas and flying spirits. In one, a single painter is restoring them, alone, by lamplight, with paints he grinds himself from stone.
events.arc: The Cave of a Thousand Buddhas

effects.log: You hold it for a whole day. The flying spirits on the ceiling seem to move in its light.
"Everyone else died, or left," he says. "The Buddhas did not leave. So I do not."
The temple guardians on the walls stand in stances that no school uses any more.

events.text: You return to the painted caves. The old restorer has found something: behind a crumbling later painting, an older one, showing a guardian performing a long sequence of moves across the whole wall, like a manual.
events.arc: The Cave of a Thousand Buddhas

ok.log: You copy all ninety-one figures. Your body learns them before your mind does.

fail.log: You copy forty before the lamp oil runs out. They are enough to keep you thinking for a year.

effects.log: It takes a season. The older painting is uncovered and the later one saved, piece by piece.

events.text: Robbers have come for the painted caves, to cut the paintings from the walls and sell them in far cities. The old restorer stands in the cave mouth with a paintbrush.
events.arc: The Cave of a Thousand Buddhas

ok.log: You use the guardian's moves from the wall. The robbers flee. The old man laughs and says the wall has been waiting for this.

fail.log: They knock you down, but in the dark of the caves they cannot find the way, and give up by dawn.

choices.text: Lead them into the wrong caves

effects.log: You lead them through the empty caves for a whole night until they leave, empty-handed and very confused.

events.text: In the burning valley of Turpan, the melons are so sweet that a farmer swears his best one is worth a horse. He is guarding it day and night in his field, because the season's melon contest is in a week.

effects.log: You sit up three nights in the field. On the third a fox tries for it. You shoo it away.

choices.text: Ask to taste a lesser melon

effects.log: It is the best thing you have ever eaten. You can only imagine the good one.
He throws a melon rind at you. It is still delicious.

events.text: On the night before the melon contest, someone has cut the prize melon from its vine. The farmer is in despair. There are small footprints in the sand, leading off towards the next farm.

ok.log: They lead to the next farm, where the rival farmer's little son is sitting with the melon, unable to lift it.

fail.log: The tracks vanish in the wind. But in the morning the melon is back on the doorstep, with an apology.

effects.log: You tell him his other melons are still magnificent. He sobs on your shoulder.

events.text: At the melon contest, the farmer's great melon takes the prize. When it is cut, he gives the first slice not to the judges but to the little boy from the next farm, who stole it to make his own father proud.

effects.log: It tastes like the whole summer of Turpan. You are given a second slice for your help.

choices.text: Persuade the two farmers to share seeds

effects.log: They grumble, then shake hands. Next year the whole valley grows champions.

events.text: A sandstorm has stripped the top off a dune in the western desert, and uncovered a city: walls, towers, a temple, all of mud brick, perfectly preserved. Nobody in the nearest town knows its name.

effects.log: Bread ovens, children's toys, a loom with the cloth still on it. They left in a hurry.
In the temple, wooden tablets in a script nobody alive can read.
The next storm covers it again. You remember the towers.

events.text: You come back to the buried city with a scholar from Dunhuang who can almost read the old script. The tablets, he says, are not prayers. They are a city's last message: a list of everyone who lived there, and where they went.

ok.log: Months of work. They went east, the tablets say, to a valley with two rivers.

fail.log: You translate only some. One of the names makes the scholar go very quiet; it is his own family's name.

choices.text: Guard the site from treasure hunters

effects.log: You camp in the gate for a season and turn away three gangs.

events.text: The scholar has followed the tablets east to a valley with two rivers, and found a village whose people still use a few words of the old script, without knowing what they are. He sends you a letter asking you to come and see.

effects.log: The villagers have a festival song that, the scholar shows you, is the city's name. They have been singing it for a thousand years.

choices.text: Send him the copy of the list

effects.log: The village elders read the names of their ancestors aloud in the square, one by one. It takes a day.

events.text: A caravan crossing the desert has a cat. Not a working cat; a fat, lazy, disdainful cat that rides on top of the lead camel and has crossed the Silk Road eleven times. The caravan master says it is the caravan's real owner.

choices.text: Pay your respects to the cat

effects.log: The cat lets you scratch its ears once. The caravan master is very impressed.

choices.text: Travel with the caravan a while

effects.log: The cat sleeps on your pack every night. It is not affection. It is ownership.
The cat ignores you too, harder.

events.text: The caravan is lost in a sandstorm. The guides have argued for a day about which way the wells are. The cat climbs down from the lead camel for the first time anyone can remember and walks off into the dunes.

effects.log: You follow it for half a day. It leads the whole caravan to a well, and drinks first.
The guides are wrong. Hours later, the cat comes back, looks at everyone with contempt, and leads them to the well.

events.text: The caravan cat has died of old age on the Silk Road. The caravan master has had it buried under a stone by the well it found, and every caravan that passes leaves a small dried fish on the stone.

effects.log: You leave one. In the night you could swear you hear something purr.
You carve a fat, disdainful cat on it. Travellers say it watches them drink.

events.text: In the far west, the river below the Kunlun mountains carries white jade down from the peaks with the snowmelt. At night, women and men wade into the cold river and feel for jade with their feet, because, they say, jade is warm at night.

choices.text: Wade in and feel for it

ok.log: Something warm under your foot. You come up with a pebble of white jade, like a frozen cloud.

fail.log: Your feet go numb. You find nothing, but the stars on the water are beautiful.

effects.log: An old picker says the best jade is the one you put back.

choices.text: Sit by the river and listen

effects.log: The river clicks and knocks as the stones move. Like a slow abacus.

events.text: An old jade picker at the White Jade River tells you of a stone the size of a horse's head, warm in winter, that lies in a pool high in the Kunlun where the river begins. Nobody has ever lifted it.

ok.log: You find it under clear water, glowing faintly. You lift it a hand's breadth, then set it down gently.

fail.log: The climb defeats you; the cold turns you back a day below the pool.

effects.log: You do not go. That night you dream of it anyway.

events.text: A merchant has hired a hundred labourers to haul the great jade stone down from the Kunlun pool. The jade pickers of the river say the river will die if it goes.

effects.log: You stand on the path with fifty pickers. The labourers are poor men; they go home when you pay them their day.

ok.log: You tell him the river's story. He climbs to the pool to see it, and comes down quiet, and calls the labourers off.

fail.log: He sneers. But the mountain sends a rockslide across the path that night, and that is the end of it.

events.text: The red Flaming Mountains of the west shimmer in the heat as if they are on fire. A local monk tells you they are the ashes of a great battle, and that a monkey once put out the fire with a fan. He sells fans.

effects.log: It is a perfectly ordinary fan. You use it all the way across the valley and are grateful.

choices.text: Climb into the mountains at noon

effects.log: The heat is like a furnace. Your qi burns. You come down a day later, tempered.
The monk laughs too. "Fans sell better with the story," he says.

events.text: Crossing the Flaming Mountains again, you find the fan-selling monk collapsed on the road from the heat, his fans scattered. His water skin is empty.

choices.text: Carry him to the next well

effects.log: You carry him on your back all afternoon, fanning him with his own fans. He wakes up at the well and tries to sell you one.
You give him every drop. You both reach the well, barely.

events.text: The fan-selling monk has a gift for you, he says: the one real fan. It is a dried palm leaf, very old, that his teacher's teacher swore was a piece of the true fan of the legend.

effects.log: It is just a palm leaf, probably. But on the hottest days it makes a breeze that seems a little too cool.

choices.text: Tell him to keep it for his business

effects.log: He laughs and keeps it, and adds you to his story. Now the monkey had help.

events.text: In a mountain gorge lives a hermit who answers every question by repeating its last three words. Pilgrims climb for days to ask him things and go away furious. You find him splitting firewood.

choices.text: Ask him the meaning of life

effects.log: "Meaning of life," he says, and splits another log. You find yourself thinking about it all the way down.
You split wood together all afternoon. Neither of you says a word. It is restful.

choices.text: Ask him why he only echoes

effects.log: "He only echoes," he agrees. You laugh, and so, very briefly, does he.

events.text: You climb back to the echoing hermit with a real question, one that has been troubling you for a long time. You find you have to phrase it very carefully, because he will only give you the end of it back.

ok.log: You end the question with the answer, without meaning to. He repeats it. You sit down hard on a log.

fail.log: You end it badly. "Go home now," he says, which might be an answer anyway.

effects.log: You sit with him until sunset. He says nothing at all. It is the best answer yet.

events.text: The echoing hermit is sick, and a crowd of pilgrims has come to hear his last words. He looks round, finds you in the crowd, and beckons. You kneel by his mat.

choices.text: Ask what he wants to say

effects.log: "You want to say," he whispers, and smiles, and is gone. You understand that the last words are yours to find.
"Thank him," he repeats, and nods towards the mountain. You bow to the mountain. It seems right.

events.text: An old hermit fishes on a river rock every day with a straight bronze pin instead of a hook, and has never caught a fish. "I am waiting for the one that wants to be caught," he says, without looking up.

effects.log: You use a proper hook and catch three fish. He watches with polite sympathy.

choices.text: Ask what fish would want that

effects.log: "The same as anyone," he says. "To be asked properly."
You leave. Behind you the line sits on the water like a thought.

events.text: You come back to the hookless fisher's rock. He has caught something: not a fish, but a young man in a fine robe who fell in the river upstream and grabbed the line, and is now dripping on the rock, swearing he is a prince.

choices.text: Help the young man dry off

effects.log: He is a prince, in fact, fleeing his brothers. The old hermit makes him tea and listens to him for three days.

choices.text: Ask the hermit if this counts

effects.log: "He wanted to be caught," the hermit says, quite satisfied.

events.text: The prince who was caught on a straight hook has become a good governor, which nobody expected. He sends an escort to fetch the old hermit to court as an advisor. The hermit asks you to go instead.

choices.text: Go to court in his place

effects.log: You advise the young governor for a season. Mostly you tell him to listen, which you learned on a river rock.

choices.text: Tell the escort he is busy fishing

effects.log: The escort goes home. The governor laughs, and sends the hermit a straight bronze pin of solid gold.
