events.text: High on a mountain path, a hut has a sign: "Soup. Pay what you think it was worth." Inside, a cheerful woman with a huge ladle says she was once the cook of a great sect, and left because they never said thank you.

effects.log: The soup is extraordinary. You pay what you have, and she laughs and gives half back.
She stares at you, then gives you a second bowl free. "First in thirty years," she says.
"Everything I know," she says. You do not get any further.

events.text: You come back to the soup hut on the mountain. The cook has a problem: her old sect has sent an elder to bring her back, because nobody there has eaten properly in thirty years. The elder is sitting in her hut, sulking.

ok.log: You get the elder to say thank you. It takes four hours and nine bowls. She agrees to cook for the sect one month a year.

fail.log: The elder refuses to thank a cook. She chases him down the mountain with the ladle.

choices.text: Eat your soup and stay out of it

effects.log: You eat, and watch the elder slowly crack over his own bowl. It is a lovely afternoon.

events.text: The mountain cook is teaching a class: a dozen young disciples from her old sect sit in her hut with spoons. Thank-yous are loud and frequent. She waves you in and gives you a bowl, and a spoon, and a seat in the class.

effects.log: You learn it, roughly. It is never quite as good as hers. People still beg you to make it.
You wash a hundred bowls. She says you have the right idea about cooking: it is mostly afterwards.

events.text: A ruined temple in the hills has no monks, no roof and no Buddha, but every dusk its bell rings. The ringer is a tiny, ancient nun who says the temple will be empty only when nobody rings it.
events.arc: The Bell Ringer of the Empty Temple

effects.log: The sound rolls down the valley. In a village below, people stop and look up.

choices.text: Ask who she rings it for

effects.log: "For the people who are listening," she says. "There is always someone."

choices.text: Repair a little of the roof

effects.log: You patch a corner over the bell. She nods, as if this was expected.

events.text: On your way past the empty temple you hear no bell at dusk. You climb up and find the old nun sitting by it, with a broken wrist from a fall, unable to swing the beam.
events.arc: The Bell Ringer of the Empty Temple

choices.text: Ring it for her every dusk this season

effects.log: You ring it for a season. The villagers below never know the ringer changed.

choices.text: Splint her wrist and ring it once

effects.log: You set the bone and ring the bell. She listens with her eyes closed.

events.text: The old nun of the empty temple has died. When you climb up at dusk, there are thirty villagers in the ruin. They had always listened. Now they have come, and nobody knows how to ring the bell.
events.arc: The Bell Ringer of the Empty Temple

effects.log: You show a farmer's boy the swing of the beam. The bell rings. A village has a temple again, without a roof.

choices.text: Ring it one last time and leave it to them

effects.log: You ring it once. When you look back from the valley road, someone is ringing it again.

events.text: On the top of a bare peak lives an old astronomer who has been counting the stars for fifty years, one patch of sky a night. He has nearly finished. He says that when he does, he will know something important.

choices.text: Count with him for a night

effects.log: You count four hundred stars in one patch of sky and lose count twice. He is patient.
"Whether there is one more than yesterday," he says. "There always is."
You leave a bundle of wood at his door. It is cold up there.

events.text: You climb back to the star counter. He has finished counting, he says, and the number is wrong: there is one star more than there should be, in the patch he counted on his first night, fifty years ago. He has been looking at it all week.

ok.log: It is very faint, low in the east. You stare until your eyes water. Something in your qi stirs, like a seed.

fail.log: You cannot find it. He shows you, patiently, again and again, until you can.

choices.text: Tell him he made a mistake fifty years ago

effects.log: "Then I have been wrong for fifty years," he says, and laughs, delighted. "That is something to know."

events.text: The star counter's new star has grown bright enough for the villagers below to see. They call it the Counter's Star. He is very old now, and asks you to keep counting after him.

effects.log: You count a patch of sky every night for a year. It is the best meditation you have ever had.

choices.text: Give the count to the villagers

effects.log: Every family takes a patch of sky. The whole valley counts stars. Children argue about them.

events.text: Woodcutters say an enormous boar rules the oak wood, a boar so old his tusks have grown into a crown. He has never hurt anyone, but nobody dares cut a tree in his wood.
events.arc: The Boar King of the Oak Wood

effects.log: You find tracks the size of plates and a tree trunk scored by tusks higher than your head.

choices.text: Ask the woodcutters what he wants

effects.log: "Acorns," says one. "And to be left alone. Like the rest of us."
You help the woodcutters in a pine wood instead. Nobody is ruled by boars there.

events.text: Deep in the oak wood at dawn, the Boar King steps out of the mist: shaggy, grey, the size of an ox, with tusks curled into a crown. He looks at you for a long time and snorts.
events.arc: The Boar King of the Oak Wood

effects.log: He walks right past you, close enough to smell. He smells of acorns and thunder.
He eats from your hands, very delicately for something so big, and grunts.

ok.log: You hold his charge for a breath. He snorts, it might be respect, and lumbers off.

fail.log: He tosses you into a thicket without much effort. He seems amused.

events.text: A lord's hunting party has come to the oak wood with dogs and spears, for the Boar King's head. The woodcutters are worried. You know where his favourite wallow is.
events.arc: The Boar King of the Oak Wood

effects.log: You send them to the far side of the wood, where they find nothing but nettles.

ok.log: You walk into his wallow and wave your arms. He looks at you, and goes deep into the wood. The hunt finds nothing.

fail.log: He does not understand, but the dogs hate the smell of you after you have been in his wallow, and refuse to hunt.

events.text: At a river ford, a turtle the size of a cart is sunning itself on the bank, its shell green with moss. Village children say it carries anyone across the river who asks politely.
events.arc: The Old Turtle of the Ford

effects.log: It considers you for a very long time, then lumbers into the water. You climb on. It carries you across.

choices.text: Scrape the moss off its shell

effects.log: It seems to enjoy this. Under the moss, its shell is carved with very old characters.
You get wet to the waist. The turtle watches you with what might be pity.

events.text: You come back to the turtle of the ford. The river is in flood, and on the far bank a family with a sick child is waiting. The ferryman will not cross. The turtle is looking at you.
events.arc: The Old Turtle of the Ford

choices.text: Ride across with it and bring them back

effects.log: It swims the flood like a rock moving underwater. The child is brought to the doctor in time.

choices.text: Swim beside it with a rope

ok.log: You swim, half carried by its wake. The family crosses on the rope. You collapse on the bank.

fail.log: The current drags at you. The turtle nudges you back to shore and goes alone.

events.text: The village by the ford has built a little roof on the bank where the old turtle suns itself. The child it carried across the flood is grown now, and is the ford's new ferryman. The turtle rides on the ferry sometimes, for the fun of it.
events.arc: The Old Turtle of the Ford

choices.text: Cross on the ferry with them

effects.log: You cross with the turtle and the ferryman, all three in the sun. It is a short, perfect crossing.

choices.text: Read the characters on its shell

effects.log: It lets you. They say: "I was old when this river was young. Be kind to it."

events.text: In a mountain forest, a white ape watches you train from a branch. When you stop, it drops to the ground and copies your stance exactly, then improves it.
events.arc: The Ape Who Learned a Stance

choices.text: Train in front of it again

effects.log: It copies every move. By evening it is better than you at all of them.
You copy it copying you. Your stance has never been steadier.
It catches it with your own guard position, eats it, and leaves.

events.text: The white ape is waiting for you at the forest edge, and leads you to a cave. On the floor, scratched into the stone over many years, are the stances of every martial artist who ever passed this mountain, copied and improved.
events.arc: The Ape Who Learned a Stance

ok.log: Dozens of schools, each with a small, simple improvement only an ape would think of. You study it for a week.

fail.log: Too much to take in. You copy what you can: a single stance that the ape has made perfect.

choices.text: Add your own stance to the floor

effects.log: You scratch your best stance in the stone. The ape studies it, and scratches a correction.

events.text: The white ape is old now and moves slowly. It brings you to the cave one last time and sits on the floor of stances, then pushes a young ape forward, who stands in your stance, perfectly.
events.arc: The Ape Who Learned a Stance

effects.log: You spend a season training with the young ape. The old one watches from the cave mouth, content.

choices.text: Seal the cave so no one finds it

effects.log: You roll a stone over the mouth, leaving a gap for apes. Some schools should only be taught by apes.

events.text: You stop at a mountain inn so perfect it cannot be real: hot baths, fine tea, a smiling innkeeper with very bright eyes, and a bill that is only one copper coin. Under the table, you notice, the innkeeper has a tail.

effects.log: The tea is the best you have ever drunk. In the morning the inn is a fox den with your coin in it.
The innkeeper turns pink, then laughs. "Nobody ever says," she says.
You leave. Behind you, the inn's lanterns go out one by one.

events.text: You find the fox inn again in a different valley. The fox innkeeper is in trouble: a monk who hunts spirits has followed her and set a trap at the gate.

effects.log: You take it apart and hide the pieces. The monk is very cross.

ok.log: You tell him about the one-copper bill. He sits down, laughs, and goes to have a bath.

fail.log: He will not listen, but while he lectures you, the fox and her inn quietly vanish.

events.text: Years later, on a cold night in the mountains, you see a lantern ahead where there should be none: the fox inn, with its door open. Inside is the spirit-hunting monk, now a regular guest, and the innkeeper waving you in.

effects.log: The best night's sleep of your life. In the morning there is a single copper coin waiting for you, with a fox stamped on it.
He tells you he hunted spirits for forty years and this is the first one he has met who was any good at tea.

events.text: At a waterfall that the locals call the Dragon Gate, carp try to leap the falls every spring. They say a carp that makes it becomes a dragon. One very small carp has been trying all morning.
events.arc: The Carp at the Dragon Gate

effects.log: It fails forty times. You cheer every time. It seems to try harder.
Ninety-one by sunset. You stop counting, but you are impressed.
You catch it. It looks at you. You put it back.

events.text: You come back to the Dragon Gate the next spring. The small carp is there, bigger now, with a scar on one fin. It is still trying. Something about it reminds you of yourself.
events.arc: The Carp at the Dragon Gate

ok.log: You leap from rock to rock up the falls as it jumps. You both reach the top. It swims off upstream without looking back.

fail.log: You fall into the pool. The carp makes it up two-thirds and falls too. You both try again.

effects.log: It makes it on the hundredth try and vanishes upstream. You find you are on your feet, shouting.

events.text: High above the Dragon Gate, in the quiet pool where the carp that make it go, you see a carp with a scarred fin, enormous now, golden in the deep water. It surfaces when you kneel by the pool.
events.arc: The Carp at the Dragon Gate

effects.log: It brushes your fingers. Whatever it is now, it remembers you.
It sinks out of sight. On the surface the ripples spread in rings, very slowly, for a long time.

events.text: A temple's sutra library has a problem: a huge white snake lives in the rafters, and the monks are too kind to kill it and too frightened to read. The library has been closed for a year.
events.arc: The Snake in the Sutra Library

ok.log: You sit under it for an hour. It comes down and coils in your lap, very heavy and cool.

fail.log: It hisses. You decide to read in a different room.

effects.log: You read for a day under its eye. It never moves. You read more carefully than you ever have.

choices.text: Advise the monks to get a cat

effects.log: They get a cat. The snake eats nothing. The cat moves into the library too.

events.text: The white snake of the sutra library has started following you around the temple. The abbot has noticed that it only coils up beside sutras that are being misread, and hisses until they are read properly.
events.arc: The Snake in the Sutra Library

choices.text: Read with the snake as a guide

effects.log: You read the whole library with a snake as your teacher. Your understanding deepens strangely.

choices.text: Let the monks study with it

effects.log: The monks are terrified and learn faster than they ever have.

events.text: The white snake of the sutra library has shed its skin, and in it, the monks say, there is a sutra: scale by scale, the pattern is characters. The abbot asks you to help read it.
events.arc: The Snake in the Sutra Library

ok.log: It is a short text on stillness, in very old characters. You read it once and feel your qi go quiet.

fail.log: You read half. The rest is beyond you. The snake seems satisfied, all the same.

choices.text: Put the skin in the library unread

effects.log: Some texts should be kept and not read. The snake curls up beside it and sleeps.

events.text: On a frozen marsh at dawn, a flock of red-crowned cranes is dancing: leaping, bowing, wings flung wide. You have seen crane styles in a dozen schools. None of them look like this.

effects.log: They dance until the sun is up. You go away with your whole body tingling.

ok.log: They let you, after a while. You leap and bow in the frost. Your lightness art will never be the same.

fail.log: They fly off, honking, very offended.

events.text: You come back to the crane marsh every winter dawn. This year the cranes are fewer: hunters have been netting them for their feathers. One lies tangled in a net in the reeds.

effects.log: You cut the net. It runs, flaps, and is gone into the sky, honking.

ok.log: You find their camp, and burn every net they own. They leave the marsh for good.

fail.log: They are gone already, but you find their nets and burn them.

events.text: At dawn on the crane marsh, the whole flock is back, bigger than ever. When they begin to dance, they open a space in the middle of the flock. It is clearly for you.

effects.log: You dance until the sun is high. When you stop, your qi moves like a crane's wing, wide and easy.
You watch them dance in the gap they left for you. It is somehow better that way.

events.text: In a mountain pass you find a tiger caught in a hunter's snare, half mad with pain. It snarls at you. Its eyes are yellow as old coins.

effects.log: You loosen the snare with a long stick. The tiger is gone in one bound, and does not look back.
You walk on. Behind you, the snarling goes on for a long time.
It takes the meat. You find the hunter and make him free it. He is not pleased.

events.text: On a lonely road at night, bandits have you surrounded. Then they look past you, and go white, and run. Behind you a tiger with yellow eyes is sitting in the road.

effects.log: It looks at you for a long time. Then it walks into the trees. You are shaking for an hour.
It flicks an ear. It might have been a nod.

events.text: At the edge of a village, a hunter shows off a tiger skin with yellow glass eyes. He says he snared it in the pass. Your heart sinks. Then you see the tiger skin is old, very old, and the hunter is a liar.

effects.log: The village laughs at him. That night, in the pass, you hear a tiger call, and smile.

choices.text: Go up to the pass to make sure

effects.log: You find tracks in the snow, big and fresh. Beside them, smaller ones. It has cubs.

events.text: A drought has lowered a mountain lake, and above the water now stands the tip of a stone gate: the gate of a sect, carved with a name you know only from old stories. The whole sect drowned when a dam broke two hundred years ago.

ok.log: Below the gate, streets and halls and a pagoda, perfect and silent under the water.

fail.log: The cold drives you back up. You saw roofs, though. Many roofs.

effects.log: The sect's rules are carved on its pillars. The last rule is: "Mind the dam."
You leave. The lake rises again in autumn.

events.text: You dive again to the sect under the lake. In the main hall, where the sect masters sat, the water is very still, and carved into the floor in front of the master's seat is a whole manual of breathing for those who must hold their breath a long time.

ok.log: You read it all before your lungs give out. The irony is not lost on you.

fail.log: You read half and surface gasping. You will have to come back.

choices.text: Bring up the sect's memorial tablets

effects.log: You bring up the tablets of the masters, one by one, so they can be honoured on dry land.

events.text: The last descendants of the drowned sect, scattered far and wide, have heard that someone found their hall. They come to the lake shore to meet you: a seamstress, a soldier, two farmers, a monk.

effects.log: You teach them on the shore. A sect has come back up out of the lake, of sorts.

choices.text: Take them to dive the gate

effects.log: One by one they touch the gate of their ancestors. The seamstress cries underwater, which is not easy.

events.text: A pine tree on a ridge has grown round an old sword: only the hilt sticks out of the trunk now, rusted brown. Locals say a swordsman drove it in a hundred years ago and swore it would come out only for someone worthy.

ok.log: It does not move at all. Then, very slightly, it does. The pine creaks.

fail.log: You pull until you see stars. Nothing. A crowd of children laughs.

effects.log: Very worn characters: "For whoever needs it." That is not quite worthy.
It looks happy there, if a sword can be happy.

events.text: You come back to the sword in the pine. A storm has split the tree, and the sword lies on the ground in the wet needles. A child from the village is standing over it, about to pick it up.

effects.log: The child lifts it high and runs home shrieking. You hope it is rusted too blunt to hurt.
It is light and perfectly balanced under the rust. You feel no one has been worthier. Or less worthy.

choices.text: Plant it back in the stump

effects.log: You drive it into the stump. Maybe the tree will grow round it again.

events.text: The old sword from the pine has been cleaned of rust. Under it, the blade is not steel at all but bronze, very old, with a line of tiny characters along the edge: the name of every person who ever carried it, and the last space is empty.

choices.text: Write a name in the empty space

effects.log: You brush a name onto the blade, one that needs it more than you. The sword goes on.
You leave the space blank. The sword will know when.

events.text: On the fifteenth night of the seventh month, on a bare hillside, a market appears: lanterns, stalls, quiet traders selling paper horses and bowls of noodles to customers who are not quite there. One stall keeper sees you and frowns. "You are early," he says.

effects.log: They taste of nothing at all, and then, suddenly, of your childhood.
"Last things," he says. "A last meal, a last word. You will want one, one day."
You walk away fast. Behind you, the market's noise fades like a dream.

events.text: On the fifteenth night of the seventh month, you go back to the hillside. The ghost market is there. The stall keeper nods to you. At another stall an old woman is trying to buy a last word and has no money.

effects.log: You pay with a coin of your own. She whispers her word into a paper cup. Somewhere a grandson wakes up, crying, and does not know why.

choices.text: Ask the stall keeper what it costs

effects.log: "A memory," he says. You give one of a sunny day. You will never miss it.

events.text: On a night that is not the seventh month at all, the ghost market's stall keeper appears at your door with a paper-wrapped parcel. "From the old woman," he says. "She had a little left over."

effects.log: It is a small cake, the kind grandmothers make. When you eat it you feel loved by someone you never met.
He comes in. The tea goes cold before he drinks it. He tells you about the market for an hour.

events.text: A mountain cave has been closed for a thousand years. An earthquake has cracked it open. Inside, every wall is carved with texts: classics, sutras, histories, recipes, martial techniques, all cut into stone so they would survive any fire.

effects.log: You read until your torch dies. A whole chapter of a lost classic, a recipe for pears.
The monks come with lamps and are speechless.
On the back wall, in big angry characters: a sword method by someone who hated swords.

events.text: You return to the stone library. Scholars from three provinces are arguing at the cave mouth about who has the right to copy it. Nobody is copying anything.

ok.log: You give each scholar a wall. In a year the library is copied. They hate you and thank you.

fail.log: They ignore you. You start copying a wall yourself. Shamed, they follow.

effects.log: Nobody else wants the recipes. You copy all two hundred. They are excellent.

events.text: The stone library has been copied, and the copies printed. In a market far away, you see a small boy reading one of the printed books, aloud, to his grandmother: a recipe for pears, from a thousand years ago.

effects.log: It is the recipe you copied. The grandmother says it sounds delicious.

choices.text: Buy them a copy of the whole set

effects.log: It costs a great deal. The boy holds it like gold.

events.text: A farmer ploughing a field has hit something huge and green with his ox: the rim of a bronze cauldron as big as a hut, buried for who knows how long. The whole village has come to stare.

effects.log: It takes all day and every spade. It is covered in faces with big round eyes, very old and very ugly.
It rings a deep note that makes the ox lie down.

choices.text: Go home before the magistrate comes

effects.log: The magistrate comes and takes the cauldron. You were wise.

events.text: The magistrate wants the great bronze cauldron sent to the capital. The village wants to keep it. It is too heavy for either. The farmer has started cooking in it, for everyone.

effects.log: Pork and turnips for three hundred. It is the best soup the village has had in years.

ok.log: You persuade the magistrate that the soup is a sacred rite. He stays for a bowl.

fail.log: He refuses. The cauldron stays anyway, because there is no cart in the province big enough.

events.text: The great bronze cauldron is now the village's festival pot. Every spring it is filled, and every traveller on the road is fed. The farmer who found it is old, and pours the first ladle for you.

effects.log: You tell the story of the day it was found. Nobody remembers it as you do. Everyone prefers your version.
Inside, under the soot, the ugly faces have been smiling all along.

events.text: In a teahouse, an old man takes off his shirt to scratch and reveals a map tattooed across his whole back: rivers, mountains, and an X. He says a pirate drew it on him when he was a boy, and he has never been able to see it.
events.arc: The Map on the Old Man's Back

effects.log: He listens, rapt. "So that is what I look like," he says.
You copy it onto paper while he drinks his tea. The X is three days from here.
He puts his shirt back on. A secret that has waited sixty years can wait.

events.text: You follow the map from the old man's back for three days to a cove. At the X there is a cave, and in it a chest, and in the chest a single child's toy and a letter.
events.arc: The Map on the Old Man's Back

effects.log: It is from the pirate, his father, saying sorry for leaving. The old man never knew.
You carry it back three days. It is very light. You do not let yourself guess.

events.text: The old man with the map on his back opens the chest in the teahouse, in front of everyone. He holds the toy for a long time. Then he laughs, and laughs, and buys tea for the whole house.
events.arc: The Map on the Old Man's Back

effects.log: He tells you about his father, whom he never met and now knows a little. It is a good afternoon.

choices.text: Ask what he will do now

effects.log: "Grow old," he says. "I was waiting for something. Now I can stop."

events.text: An old brick pagoda on a hill leans so far that it should have fallen centuries ago. People come from everywhere to stand underneath it and feel brave. Inside, on every floor, is a statue facing the opposite way from the lean.

effects.log: The top floor leans like a ship's mast. The view is wonderful and you hold on very tight.

ok.log: The statues are counterweights, arranged as a formation. Someone very clever is holding the pagoda up.

fail.log: You work it out partly. Enough to be uneasy standing under it.

effects.log: You do. It is surprisingly effective.

events.text: A monk has decided to straighten the leaning pagoda by turning the statues to face the right way. He has turned one. The pagoda has groaned, and dust is falling.

effects.log: You turn it. The groaning stops. The monk is offended, then very pale.
You clear the hill. The pagoda groans all night. In the morning it is still standing, a little more bent.

events.text: The leaning pagoda has stood another year. The repentant monk now sweeps around the statues every day, careful not to touch them. He has written a sign: "These statues are holding the pagoda up. So, probably, is somebody's prayer."

choices.text: Add a prayer of your own

effects.log: You add yours. You feel, for no reason you can name, that it helps.
It is beautiful. You learn more about balance from a leaning building than from any book.

events.text: In a high valley there is a pond so still it reflects the sky perfectly. But the clouds in the pond are not the clouds in the sky. They are tomorrow's.

effects.log: Tomorrow the clouds are exactly as the pond said. You feel dizzy.
Your reflection looks a day older. It seems to be in a good mood.
The ripples blur tomorrow. You feel you have done something rude.

events.text: You come back to the pond that shows tomorrow. Today the pond shows smoke rising from the village below the valley, and people running.

effects.log: You warn them. Nobody believes you, but they carry water to the granary anyway, to humour you. That night a fire starts, and is out in moments.
Tomorrow there is a fire, as the pond said, and a hard day. You help put it out, and never forgive yourself.

events.text: The pond that shows tomorrow has gone cloudy. When you kneel beside it, the cloudiness clears, and it shows only your own face, today's, looking back.

effects.log: Tomorrow will be what you make it. You understand the pond is done with you.
It shows you nothing. You laugh, and go home. Some answers are enough.

events.text: In a certain village, everyone has one shoe. Every night, a single shoe vanishes from somebody's doorstep. The villagers blame foxes, spirits, the magistrate and each other.

effects.log: At midnight a small brown shape slips past with a shoe in its mouth. You lose it in the dark.

choices.text: Leave your own shoe out as bait

effects.log: It is gone by morning. You walk the village in one shoe, like everyone else.
You move on. Your shoes are both still on your feet. For now.

events.text: You follow the small brown shape from the shoe village into the woods. It is a dog, an old one, carrying a shoe to a hollow under a fallen tree, where there are hundreds of shoes, and a single puppy asleep on them.

choices.text: Return the shoes to the village

effects.log: You bring back four hundred shoes. Some have been missing for years. The village throws a feast.
You leave the shoes and bring the dog bones instead. The thieving stops. Mostly.

events.text: The old shoe-thieving dog has died, and the village has adopted its puppy, now grown, who brings everyone their shoes in the morning instead. Each shoe is a little damp. They are thrilled.

effects.log: It brings you a shoe that is not yours, proudly. You keep it.

choices.text: Carve a statue of the old dog

effects.log: You carve a small wooden dog with a shoe in its mouth. The village puts it at the gate.

events.text: The drum tower of a small town rings the hours late: always exactly one quarter of an hour late, for as long as anyone remembers. The whole town keeps time by it, and is late for everything.

effects.log: The water clock is perfect. The bell ringer is not there. The bell rings anyway, late.
"It has always been late," they say. "We like it. Nobody hurries."

choices.text: Set your own pace by it

effects.log: You are late for everything for a week. It is very relaxing.

events.text: You have worked out the bell that rings late: the ringer is an old woman who lives in the tower base, and she rings it late because her husband always came home a quarter hour after the bell, and she wanted to hear it when he did.

effects.log: You say nothing. The town goes on being late, contentedly.
The town is quiet. Then the elders decide the bell will go on being late, forever, by law.

events.text: The old bell ringer has died. The town has a new ringer, young and precise. On the first night, the bell rings on the hour. The whole town comes out into the street, uneasy.

choices.text: Ask the ringer to ring it late

effects.log: The young ringer listens to the story and rings it late from then on. The town sleeps easy.
They vote. Late wins by a landslide. The ringer sighs and adjusts the water clock.

events.text: In an alley in a city, someone has painted a door on a blank brick wall: so well that people walk into it. Every week the painting changes slightly. The latest version has a doorknob.
events.arc: The Door Painted on a Wall

effects.log: At midnight a girl with a paint pot and a ladder comes and adds a doormat.
Your knuckles hit brick. A window opens above you. "It is not finished!" someone shouts.
You walk past. You notice, for the first time, how many doors in the city are real.

events.text: The girl who paints the door on the alley wall has finished it. It is extraordinary: you would swear it is ajar, with light behind it. The landlord wants it painted over. The alley wants it to stay.
events.arc: The Door Painted on a Wall

ok.log: You persuade him to come and see it at dusk. He reaches for the knob, and laughs, and leaves it.

fail.log: He refuses, so the alley pays the rent on the wall. You chip in.

effects.log: You pay her to paint one on your own wall. It is the best money you have ever spent.

events.text: The door painter of the alley has become famous: there are painted doors all over the city now, and travellers come to walk into them. Her first door is still there, and someone has worn the brick shiny where the knob is.
events.arc: The Door Painted on a Wall

effects.log: It is warm from all the hands. You feel, very briefly, that the door might open.

choices.text: Find the painter and thank her

effects.log: She is surprised you remember. She paints a small door on your sleeve, for luck.

events.text: On a rainy road you find an oiled-paper umbrella open and upright in the middle of the road, keeping a small patch of ground dry. There is nobody near it.

effects.log: You walk under it. It is perfectly dry inside, and seems to tilt to keep the rain off you.
You walk round it. When you look back, it is still there, dry ground beneath.
In the dry patch there is a sparrow, sheltering. It looks offended.

events.text: The umbrella from the road always opens itself when it is going to rain, a little before the rain comes. Today it is opening and closing, opening and closing, by the door, as if it wants to go somewhere.

effects.log: It leads you to a crossroads where an old man is standing in the rain looking for something. "My umbrella," he says.
It goes on twitching for a week, then gives up and sulks in the corner.

events.text: The old man of the crossroads made the umbrella for his wife, who died, and lost it on the road. He gives it back to you. "It likes you," he says. "And it never liked me."

effects.log: You keep the umbrella all your life. You never once get wet, which some people find suspicious.

choices.text: Give it to a soaked child

effects.log: You give it to a child in the rain. It tilts towards them at once. The old man nods.

events.text: On a mountain path, a stone shrine the size of a cupboard is locked with a bronze lock, and the key is lost. Every passing traveller tries to open it. It has never opened. Its door is polished smooth from hands.

ok.log: Your fingers find the pins as if they were acupoints. It clicks. You stop, not sure you should go on.

fail.log: It does not open. Nothing, it seems, opens it.

choices.text: Leave an offering on the step

effects.log: You leave rice. Something inside clicks, very softly. You decide you imagined it.
You walk on. It is a long way to the top.

events.text: You come back to the locked shrine. Today it is unlocked, door slightly open, the lock lying on the step. Inside there is only a mirror, and a slip of paper: "For you."

effects.log: You see yourself. Only that. You stand there a long time.
You take it. Who else is it for?
You snap the lock shut. The next traveller should have the chance.

events.text: A child on the mountain path asks you, very seriously, what is inside the shrine with no key. Everyone has told the child a different story. The child wants the true one.

effects.log: "A mirror," you say. The child thinks about it, and nods, and looks happy, and you do not quite know why.

choices.text: Tell the child to find out

effects.log: "When it opens for you," you say. The child runs off up the path, determined.

events.text: Between two peaks there is a gorge with no bridge. But in thick fog, the woodcutters say, a bridge appears. This morning the fog is thick, and there it is: an old rope bridge, swaying, leading into the grey.
events.arc: The Bridge That Is Only There in Fog

ok.log: The other side is a bare peak with a small hut and a garden, and nobody in it.

fail.log: Halfway, the fog thins, and the bridge with it. You run back and reach the edge as it vanishes.

effects.log: The fog lifts and the bridge goes with it, plank by plank, as if it was never there.
From the other side, very faint, someone shouts back: "Come in, the tea is hot."

events.text: You cross the fog bridge again. The hut on the far peak is occupied now: a grey-haired woman is drinking tea in the garden. She says she built the bridge herself, a long time ago, out of fog and stubbornness.
events.arc: The Bridge That Is Only There in Fog

effects.log: She teaches you to breathe the way fog moves. It takes a whole season. Your qi grows soft and endless.
You talk all day. She has been everywhere. The fog thins; she sends you home before it goes.

events.text: The fog bridge has not appeared all year. When it finally does, it is fainter, more fog than rope. On the far side, the woman's hut is closed, and on its door is a note for you.
events.arc: The Bridge That Is Only There in Fog

effects.log: "The bridge is yours now. Mind the fog." You cross it often afterwards, alone, and it holds.

choices.text: Leave the bridge to the fog

effects.log: You do not cross. You watch it fade into the mountain, and feel lighter.

events.text: On the ferry road, a single white goose has made itself the toll keeper. It stands in the middle of the road and attacks anyone who does not give it bread. Grown men walk an extra li to avoid it.
events.arc: The Goose of the Ferry Road

effects.log: It accepts the bread and honks you through. You feel strangely honoured.

ok.log: You stand your ground. The goose respects this, barely, and lets you pass.

fail.log: The goose wins. You lose your hat and some dignity.

effects.log: You walk the extra li. You meet three grown men doing the same.

events.text: The goose of the ferry road has been joined by its family: a mate and six goslings, all in the road, all demanding bread. A magistrate's procession is coming, and the magistrate is terrified of geese.
events.arc: The Goose of the Ferry Road

choices.text: Hand out bread to clear the road

effects.log: You feed eight geese while the procession creeps past. The magistrate bows to you from his chair.

ok.log: You herd them into a field with great dignity. Everyone applauds.

fail.log: The geese herd you instead. The magistrate takes the long way round.

events.text: The village by the ferry road has made the goose their official toll keeper, with a little wooden hut and a sign. The toll goes to the village school. The goose has grown fat and terrible and is very proud.
events.arc: The Goose of the Ferry Road

effects.log: You pay in bread. The goose remembers you and only hisses once.
The schoolmaster thanks you. The goose hisses at you anyway, out of principle.

events.text: A boy has followed you for three li, convinced you are a legendary hermit master he has been searching for. He has a drawing. It looks nothing like you. He will not be told.

effects.log: You teach him a basic stance. He weeps with joy and calls you Master of the Crimson Peak.

choices.text: Insist you are not the master

effects.log: He nods, wisely, and says that is just what the master would say.
You run. He follows, slower. You lose him at a river.

events.text: The boy who thinks you are the Master of the Crimson Peak is back, with ten friends, all wanting to be your disciples. The real Master of the Crimson Peak has also heard about you, and wants a word.

ok.log: The real master is a tiny old woman who finds the whole thing hilarious. She offers to share the boys.

fail.log: The real master is very cross. You end up doing her laundry for a month to make amends.

choices.text: Hand the boys over to her at once

effects.log: You walk the boys up the Crimson Peak yourself. She is amused. The boys are confused.

events.text: The boy who followed you is a young man now, and a disciple of the real Master of the Crimson Peak. He has come to thank you. He knew all along you were the wrong master, he says. He just liked the way you taught.

effects.log: He has become very good. You hold your own, just. You both end up laughing on the grass.

choices.text: Ask the old master how he did

effects.log: "He calls me the wrong master too," she says. "It is a compliment."

events.text: A white-bearded sage in flowing robes is stuck in the top of a pine tree, very calmly. He says he climbed it to meditate on impermanence and has been meditating on the problem of getting down for two days.
events.arc: The Sage Stuck in the Tree

choices.text: Climb up and help him down

ok.log: You bring him down on your back. He thanks you and climbs a smaller tree at once.

fail.log: You both get stuck. You meditate together until a woodcutter fetches a ladder.

choices.text: Ask him what he has learned

effects.log: "That going up is a decision," he says, "and coming down is a negotiation."
You bring a ladder. He refuses it, on principle, for an hour, then accepts.

events.text: The sage who was stuck in the pine tree has founded a school of meditation based entirely on climbing trees. His students are in trees all over the hillside. Several of them are stuck.
events.arc: The Sage Stuck in the Tree

effects.log: You spend a day lifting students out of trees. The sage watches, proud.

choices.text: Join the school for a week

effects.log: You meditate in a tree for a week. Your balance becomes uncanny.

events.text: The sage of the tree school has died, at a great age, peacefully, at the very top of the tallest pine. Nobody can get him down. His students have decided he would want to stay there.
events.arc: The Sage Stuck in the Tree

effects.log: You climb. At the top, the view is wide and the wind is kind. You understand why he stayed.

choices.text: Teach the students to climb down

effects.log: You teach them coming down, which he never did. It is, they agree, the harder half.

events.text: On a bridge in a market town, two noodle stalls face each other, run by two brothers who have not spoken in twenty years. Both are excellent. Both demand you say which is better.

choices.text: Eat at both and praise both

effects.log: Both brothers are furious with you. Both give you an extra egg.
The younger brother throws a dumpling at you. It is delicious.
Both brothers stare at you as if you are mad.

events.text: Back on the noodle bridge, you learn why the brothers quarrelled: their mother's broth recipe, which each of them believes the other stole. Their mother is still alive, ninety, and refuses to settle it.

ok.log: She laughs till she coughs. "I gave each half the recipe," she says. "So they would need each other."

fail.log: She refuses to tell you either, but gives you a bowl of the real thing. It is perfect.

effects.log: You notice each is missing exactly what the other has.

events.text: The old mother of the noodle brothers is dying, and she has asked for one bowl of her own broth. Neither brother can make it alone. They are standing in the same kitchen for the first time in twenty years, not looking at each other.

effects.log: You pass ingredients back and forth until they are cooking together. She drinks her bowl and smiles.

choices.text: Leave them alone in the kitchen

effects.log: You leave. An hour later you hear shouting, then laughing, then quiet.

events.text: At a scenic waterfall, a scholar is reciting a poem about it so bad that the birds have left. He asks your opinion. The poem rhymes "waterfall" with "waterfall" four times.
events.arc: The Worst Poet in the Province

effects.log: He is overjoyed and recites twelve more. You survive.
He is crushed, then thoughtful, then asks how to improve.
You recite one. He weeps, says he will never write again, and starts a new one at once.

events.text: The worst poet in the province has entered the governor's poetry contest, with a poem about you. You are in the audience. It is very long.
events.arc: The Worst Poet in the Province

effects.log: The audience, startled, follows your lead. He takes ninth place out of nine and is ecstatic.

choices.text: Slip him a better last line

ok.log: Your line saves the poem. He takes fourth place and owes you forever.

fail.log: He mixes it up with his own line and it rhymes "you" with "you". The crowd groans.

events.text: The worst poet in the province has published a book of poems. It is still very bad. But it has sold out: people buy it to read aloud at parties, and laugh, and then go quiet at the last poem, which is about his mother, and is good.
events.arc: The Worst Poet in the Province

effects.log: You read the last poem three times. Then the others, laughing, in front of the waterfall.
He writes a dedication to you that rhymes "friend" with "friend". It is the nicest thing.

events.text: An enormous ox is galloping down the village street, pursued by a very small farmer shouting "Little Plum! Little Plum!" It is heading straight for the market.

ok.log: You grab the horns and dig in your heels. You slide twenty feet but it stops, just short of the egg seller.

fail.log: It carries you into the market on its horns and stops at the cabbage stall on its own, very pleased.

choices.text: Clear people out of its way

effects.log: You shout and wave. The market clears. The ox gallops through and out the other side.
You leap aside. It thunders past. You are fine. The cabbages are not.

events.text: The ox called Little Plum has escaped again, and this time it has run up a mountain and will not come down. The small farmer is beside himself. He says it only listens to people it likes, and it likes you.

choices.text: Climb up and talk to it

effects.log: You find it eating flowers at the top, happy. It follows you down like a dog.
You carry a cabbage up the mountain. Little Plum follows the cabbage down.

events.text: Little Plum the ox has won first prize at the county fair, as the biggest ox in three provinces. The small farmer insists you lead it round the ring, because it will not walk for anyone else.

effects.log: It walks perfectly, then sits down in the middle and refuses to move. The crowd loves it.
You ride Little Plum round the ring like a general. Children scream with joy.

events.text: On a snowy hillside a single plum tree is in full flower, red as fire against the white. There is a small pavilion beside it with a stone bench, as if someone built it for exactly this.

effects.log: You sit until the cold gets into your bones. The plum blossom falls on the snow like small red thoughts.
You write one line on the pavilion pillar in charcoal. It is not bad.

choices.text: Shake the snow off the branches

effects.log: The tree sighs, lighter. Petals and snow fall on you together.

events.text: You come back to the plum tree in the snow the next winter. Under your line on the pavilion pillar, someone has written a second line, answering yours.

ok.log: You write it. It is the best line you have ever written. You go home warm.

fail.log: You write something clumsy. Next winter it has been gently corrected.

choices.text: Wait to see who wrote it

effects.log: Nobody comes, all day. You leave a cup of tea on the bench for them.

events.text: Year after year, the poem on the pillar of the snow pavilion has grown, a line each winter, yours and the stranger's. Now the pillar is full. This winter there is a last line in the stranger's hand: "Thank you for the company."

effects.log: You copy it out. It is a whole life, in winters. You keep it always.

choices.text: Plant another plum tree beside the first

effects.log: You plant a sapling and build a second bench. For the next pair of strangers.

events.text: At dusk in a summer valley, the fireflies come out: first one, then ten, then so many the valley glows like a lantern festival with no lanterns. A small girl is catching them in a jar.

effects.log: You catch fifty. She lets them go all at once, and laughs.

choices.text: Lie in the grass and watch

effects.log: The stars come out above and the fireflies below. You cannot tell where one ends.

choices.text: Tell her to let them go

effects.log: She lets them go, slowly, one by one, saying goodbye to each.

events.text: The girl from the firefly valley says the fireflies are fewer this year: the stream where they hatch has been dammed for a mill, and the reeds are dying.

choices.text: Help her talk to the miller

effects.log: The miller is gruff, but he has a daughter too. He opens a channel round the mill.
You dig for a week with the girl and her brothers. The reeds turn green again.

events.text: Summer comes again in the firefly valley, and the fireflies are back, more than ever. The miller and his daughter, the girl and her brothers and half the village are sitting in the grass in the dark.

effects.log: Nobody speaks. The valley glows. It is one of the best evenings of your life.

choices.text: Catch one firefly and let it go

effects.log: It lights on your fingertip, blinks twice, and drifts away. The girl claps.

events.text: A waterfall in a green gorge falls like a curtain over a cliff. Behind it, the locals say, there is a cave, but nobody has ever been brave enough to go through the water.

ok.log: The water pounds you flat for a heartbeat. Then you are through, in a cave of green light.

fail.log: The water knocks you into the pool. You come up laughing.

effects.log: In the dry season the waterfall is a trickle. You walk into the cave with dry feet.
The water is cold and clear. You float on your back and watch the spray make rainbows.

events.text: In the cave behind the waterfall, the light through the falling water is green and gold and always moving. On the wall, someone long ago has painted a single line of characters.

effects.log: "Be still. You are already hidden." You sit down and are, for an afternoon, entirely still.
You sit with your eyes closed. The roar of the water becomes a silence. You open your eyes calmer than ever.

events.text: You come back to the waterfall cave when you need to be still. It has become yours, in the way a place can be. Today there is a young traveller in it, soaked and frightened, hiding from someone.

choices.text: Let them stay and keep quiet

effects.log: You sit together in silence until whoever was hunting the young traveller has gone. You never learn who.

choices.text: Show them the line on the wall

effects.log: They read it, and breathe out, and are still. When they leave they bow to the wall, not to you.

events.text: In autumn, a valley in the hills turns red: every maple at once, as if someone set it alight. A temple at the valley head holds a viewing every year, and this year its old monk has fallen ill.

choices.text: Help the temple with the viewing

effects.log: You sweep paths, carry tea, and lead old people to the best rocks. It is the busiest and best day of your autumn.
He is in bed by the window, watching the maples. "I have seen seventy," he says. "They are always new."
You walk among red leaves all day. Your heart feels scrubbed clean.

events.text: The old monk of the red valley asks you to take him up to the ridge to see the maples from above, one last time. He is too weak to walk.

effects.log: You carry him to the ridge. Below, the valley burns red. He says nothing for an hour, then: "Thank you."

choices.text: Build a chair and carry it with others

effects.log: Four of you carry him up. He laughs at the bumps. At the top he goes quiet.

events.text: The old monk of the red valley has died, and a young monk keeps the temple. He shows you the old man's last wish, written on a slip of paper: that the person who carried him to the ridge should lead the autumn viewing this year.

effects.log: You lead a thousand people through the red valley. It feels like carrying him again.

choices.text: Lead it and then hand it on

effects.log: You lead it once and teach the young monk how. Next year he does it, nervously, well.

events.text: At night in a bamboo grove you hear a flute, playing a tune so sad and lovely you stop walking. You cannot see the player. The music seems to come from the bamboo itself.

effects.log: You follow it in circles all night. At dawn it stops. You are exactly where you started.
You sing back. The flute pauses, then plays your tune, better.
You listen until it stops. You do not know why you are crying, but it is not unhappy.

events.text: Back in the bamboo grove you find the flute player: a single cracked bamboo stem, through which the night wind blows with exactly that sad lovely note. Beside it, someone has carved a name and a date, eighty years old.

choices.text: Cut a flute from the stem

effects.log: You cut a flute. It plays only the one tune, but plays it perfectly.
You leave it. Some music is better left to the wind.

events.text: In a town, an old man hears you play the bamboo flute's tune and stops dead in the street. He says he carved his name on that stem eighty years ago, the night he said goodbye to someone forever, and has never heard the tune since.

effects.log: He plays it, badly, for the first time in eighty years. Then he weeps and gives it back.

choices.text: Play it for him to the end

effects.log: You play the tune to its end. He thanks you and walks away much straighter.

events.text: On a plateau above the clouds is a stone floor a thousand paces across, scarred with sword cuts deep as ditches. Two masters fought here for nine days a thousand years ago, the story says, and the stone still remembers every stroke.
events.arc: The Duelling Ground of the Ancients

effects.log: You walk them in order, as they were made. By evening your arm aches as if you fought the duel yourself.

choices.text: Sit in the centre and listen

effects.log: The wind in the cuts makes a sound like steel. Your qi answers it.
You leave. Some duels should be left finished.

events.text: Walking the ancient duelling ground again, you find what nobody else has noticed: the last stroke of the nine-day duel was never made. The two masters' final cuts stop a finger's breadth apart.
events.arc: The Duelling Ground of the Ancients

ok.log: Neither of them struck. They stopped. You sit down where they stood and laugh, at last understanding.

fail.log: You puzzle for a week and decide they ran out of strength. You are not sure you believe yourself.

effects.log: You cut the stone where the last stroke should be. The plateau is silent. You feel you have been rude.

events.text: Two young masters have come to the ancient duelling ground to fight to the death over an insult. They have heard the stories and want to be remembered like the ancients.
events.arc: The Duelling Ground of the Ancients

effects.log: You show them the two cuts that stop short. They stare a long time, and sheathe their swords.

ok.log: You disarm them both. They are humiliated, then grateful, then your friends.

fail.log: They are good, and together they push you back, but by then they have forgotten why they were fighting.

events.text: A bare black peak draws every storm in the province: lightning strikes its top a hundred times a night. On the summit, the rock has turned to glass. Martial artists who seek the thunder arts sometimes climb it. Few come back down quickly.

ok.log: You reach the top as the lightning falls. The air smells of iron. Your qi crackles for a month.

fail.log: Halfway up, a strike knocks you flat. You crawl down with your hair standing on end.

effects.log: The glass summit is beautiful in the sun, like ice. You find a ring of footprints melted into it.
A hundred bolts in a night. You count them, and your qi trembles with each.

events.text: On the glass summit of the thunder peak, you find the footprints melted into the rock again, and understand them: they are a stance, a stepping pattern, made by someone who stood here in a storm and moved so the lightning missed them.

choices.text: Learn the steps in a storm

ok.log: Lightning falls round you like rain. You step, and step, and it misses. You come down shaking and changed.

fail.log: You learn half and the storm passes. You will need another.

effects.log: Safer, slower. In a year you have the pattern, if not the thunder.

events.text: A young disciple is trying to climb the thunder peak in a storm, alone, without the steps. You see the tiny figure on the ridge from far below, and the storm is gathering.

choices.text: Climb up and bring them down

effects.log: You reach the disciple just in time and step them both down through the lightning. They never forget it.

choices.text: Climb up and teach them the steps

effects.log: You teach the disciple in the storm itself, step by step. They make it to the top. So do you.

events.text: In a glacier in the far mountains, under clear blue ice, sits a martial artist in meditation, perfectly preserved, robes and all. Mountain people bring him offerings. Nobody knows how long he has been there.

effects.log: You sit before the ice for three days. On the third, you are almost sure he is breathing.
His posture is a breathing method you have never seen. You copy it.
You leave rice cakes. The mountain people nod at you approvingly.

events.text: You come back to the master in the ice. The glacier has moved, and he is closer to the surface now. In the ice before him, you see, his finger is pointing at something: a single word scratched in the ice by his nail.

ok.log: "Wait." You sit down again. For the first time in your life, waiting feels like an art.

fail.log: The ice blurs it. You make out the first stroke and decide it can only be one word.

effects.log: You chip for a day and stop. Something tells you not yet.

events.text: The glacier has broken open at last. The master who sat in the ice for longer than anyone knows opens his eyes, breathes in, and looks at you. "Who rules now?" he asks, very politely.

effects.log: You talk until night. He listens, nods, and says: "Then nothing has changed." He walks off down the mountain, cheerful.

choices.text: Ask what he was waiting for

effects.log: "For someone to sit with me," he says. "It took a while." He bows to you and leaves.
He teaches you one breath. Only one. It is worth a year of any master's teaching.

events.text: In a valley no road reaches, thousands of swords stand point-down in the earth, rusted, overgrown with grass. A sword master of old is said to have buried here every sword he ever defeated.

effects.log: Thousands of swords. Some still have tassels, faded to grey. The silence is enormous.

ok.log: At the centre, a plain blade with no ornament, the only one not rusted.

fail.log: You search until dark and find only rust.

choices.text: Plant your own old sword there

effects.log: You plant your oldest blade among them. It feels like retiring something.

events.text: You come back to the valley of swords. A young swordsman is digging up the rusted blades one by one, looking for the master's plain sword. He says it is his by right of blood.

ok.log: You spar. He is not bad. The plain sword, when he finds it, will not leave the earth for him.

fail.log: He is better than you thought. You both stop, panting, and he admits he has no claim at all.

effects.log: You help him. By sunset he has dug up a hundred rusty swords and is ashamed. He plants them back.

events.text: The young swordsman of the valley of swords has stayed, to tend it. He has made the swords a garden: cleaned the tassels, cut the grass, written each sword's school on a stone at its foot. He shows you round proudly.

effects.log: You name thirty of them. He carves every name. The valley feels less lonely.

choices.text: Teach him a form among the swords

effects.log: You teach him among the blades. He learns fast. The swords seem to watch.

events.text: In the middle of a perfectly still lake there is an island with a single pavilion. There are no boats. Locals say you can walk to it on the moon's reflection, on the one night a year it lies straight across the water.
events.arc: The Island in the Lake of Mirrors

ok.log: You run along the silver path and reach the island with dry feet, laughing.

fail.log: You make it three steps and sink. You swim back, very cold.

effects.log: You swim. The water is warmer than you expected. The pavilion is empty, swept, waiting.

choices.text: Watch the moon path from the shore

effects.log: It lies straight across the water, then bends, then breaks. Beautiful.

events.text: In the pavilion on the island in the lake, a table is set for two with cups, a teapot, and a board for weiqi. It has been set like this, the dust says, for a very long time. A note says: "For whoever comes."
events.arc: The Island in the Lake of Mirrors

effects.log: You wait all night. Nobody comes. You drink both cups, and play both sides of a game. It is peaceful.

choices.text: Clean the pavilion and reset the table

effects.log: You clean, and reset, and add a note of your own: "I came."

events.text: Years later, you return to the island pavilion. Under your note someone has written: "So did I." And a second hand: "And I." A third, a fourth, a fifth. The table is set again for two.
events.arc: The Island in the Lake of Mirrors

effects.log: You write: "Again." You leave the tea for the next.
At dusk, a stranger rows up in a small boat and sits down across from you, smiling. You play until morning.

events.text: A narrow waterfall falls so hard and straight it cuts a groove in the rock below like a blade. Swordsmen come to stand under it and feel the cut. Most are knocked flat.

ok.log: You stand. It hammers your shoulders. For a heartbeat you feel what it is to be a blade.

fail.log: It flattens you into the pool. You come up spluttering.

effects.log: Straight, patient, endless. It took a thousand years. You think about your own training.
The pool is lovely. Swordsmen keep landing in it.

events.text: Standing under the cutting waterfall again, you notice a sword hilt wedged in a crack in the rock behind it, polished by water for who knows how many years. Someone hid it there, where only those who stand under the falls would ever see.

ok.log: It comes out with a shriek of stone: a blade worn so thin by the water it is almost transparent.

fail.log: It will not move. You must stand under the falls longer.

effects.log: The falls are still sharpening it. You will come back.

events.text: The water-worn blade from behind the falls cuts nothing you swing it at; it is too thin. But held still in running water, it parts the stream so cleanly that the two halves never touch again.

choices.text: Practise with it in the river

effects.log: You learn to cut without force. Your swordsmanship becomes quieter and more dangerous.
You put it back in the crack. Somebody else should stand under the water long enough to find it.

events.text: By a river a monk is writing with a big brush dipped in plain water on a flat river stone. The characters dry in moments and vanish. He has been doing this every day for forty years.
events.arc: The Monk Who Writes on Water

effects.log: You read one sutra before it vanishes. You never forget it.
"Ink would be pride," he says. "Water is practice."
You write your name in water on the stone. It is gone before you finish. You laugh.

events.text: The monk who writes on water hands you the brush. "Write the thing you most regret," he says. "And then watch it go."
events.arc: The Monk Who Writes on Water

effects.log: You write it. It dries in the sun and is gone. Something in your chest eases that has been tight for years.

choices.text: Write something you are grateful for

effects.log: You write it. It vanishes too. "That one comes back," the monk says. "That is the trick."

events.text: The monk who writes on water has died, and his stone by the river is bare. Every morning now, travellers stop, dip a finger in the river, and write something on it, and watch it go.
events.arc: The Monk Who Writes on Water

choices.text: Write one last thing for him

effects.log: You write his name. It dries and is gone, as he would want.

choices.text: Teach a child to write on the stone

effects.log: You teach a fisher's child. They write their first character in water and are amazed it is gone.

events.text: In an abandoned courtyard, there is an old well so deep that, even at noon, you can see stars in the water at the bottom. Children dare each other to drop a coin and make a wish.

effects.log: It falls for a very long time. You never hear it land. You feel lucky anyway.

choices.text: Lower a lantern on a rope

effects.log: The rope runs out. The lantern hangs in the dark, and still the stars are below it.
Your echo comes back a long time later, in a slightly different voice.

events.text: Coins are coming up from the well of stars: children find them on the courtyard stones in the mornings, old coins, very old, from dynasties gone a thousand years. One morning, a coin is yours, the one you dropped.

effects.log: You keep it in your sleeve. It is always warm.
You drop it again. "Not yet," you say to the well. You do not know why.

events.text: The courtyard of the well of stars has been bought by a merchant who wants to fill in the well and build a warehouse. The children of the street are sitting round it in protest.

ok.log: He sells it for a fair sum, surprised. The children are now landowners, under your name.

fail.log: He asks too much. You pay it. The children cheer. Your purse weeps.

effects.log: You sit for three days. On the third, the merchant looks into the well, sees the stars at noon, and leaves.

events.text: Beyond the last village the land turns white: a salt lake, dry and flat as paper, with a thin skin of water that mirrors the sky so perfectly you seem to walk on clouds.

effects.log: You walk until the shore is gone. Sky above, sky below. You have never felt so small or so calm.

choices.text: Gather salt with the salt makers

effects.log: You rake salt with them all day. Your hands sting. Supper is very well seasoned.

choices.text: Watch the sunset from the shore

effects.log: The whole lake turns pink, then gold, then the colour of a lantern.

events.text: In the middle of the white salt lake you find a cairn of salt blocks, and on top of it a pair of old straw sandals, and a note under a stone: "I walked out to see if the sky ends. It does not. Please look after my goats."

effects.log: At the lake shore, a small, patient herd is waiting by an empty hut. You take them to the village.
You add salt blocks until it can be seen from the shore. A marker for the next walker.

events.text: At the white salt lake, the goat herd has grown, kept by a village child who calls you their owner. Under the cairn on the lake, someone has left a second pair of sandals, and a note in a new hand: "It does not end. I am going on."

effects.log: You write: "The goats are fine." You walk home on the clouds.
You walk out across the salt for a day and come back. The sky does not end. That is all right.

events.text: On a Jiangnan canal at night, an old boatwoman poles a little boat loaded with paper lanterns, setting one adrift under every bridge. She says each is for someone who drowned in the canal, and she knows all their names.

effects.log: You light lanterns until your fingers are black. She tells you a name for each.
"I pulled most of them out," she says. "I was not always quick enough."
The lanterns drift beneath you like slow stars.

events.text: The old boatwoman of the canal lanterns is too weak to pole her boat. She asks you to set the lanterns this year, and gives you the list of names, written on a long scroll.

choices.text: Set every lantern and say every name

effects.log: It takes all night. At dawn the canal is full of light.

ok.log: You learn all three hundred. You never forget one.

fail.log: You learn most. You read the rest, carefully.

events.text: The boatwoman has died. You set her lanterns again and, at the end of the scroll, add one name more. Behind you, from every bridge, townspeople are setting lanterns of their own.

choices.text: Keep the boat going every year

effects.log: You pole the lantern boat each year you can. It becomes the town's festival.

choices.text: Hand the boat to a young boatwoman

effects.log: A young ferry girl takes the pole. She is quick. Nobody drowns in her years.

events.text: South of the mountains is a forest made of stone: grey pillars of rock taller than pagodas, crowded so close you can get lost in an hour. A herd girl says her goat went in yesterday and has not come out.

ok.log: You follow its droppings for half a day. It is standing on top of a stone pillar, very pleased with itself.

fail.log: You get lost. The herd girl finds you, and the goat, by evening, and laughs at both of you.

effects.log: From the top, the stone forest is a sea of grey spires. You spot the goat on another spire, staring at you.

events.text: Back in the stone forest, you follow the climbing goat deeper than anyone goes and find a ring of pillars with carvings on them: a calendar, the herd girl says, made by her ancestors to know when to plant.

effects.log: You copy it. A farmer's almanac, a thousand years old and more accurate than the magistrate's.

choices.text: Let the girl read it to you

effects.log: She reads it as if it were a story. To her, it is.

events.text: The herd girl's village has started planting by the stone calendar again. This year their harvest is the best in the county, and the magistrate wants to know their secret. The goat is wearing a garland.

choices.text: Let the village keep its secret

effects.log: You say nothing to the magistrate. The goat looks at you approvingly.
Every village in the county plants by the stone forest now. Nobody goes hungry that winter.

events.text: At a great horse fair on the frontier, ten thousand horses are bought and sold in a cloud of dust. A boy is trying to sell an ugly, shaggy, bad-tempered pony nobody wants.

effects.log: It costs almost nothing. It bites you at once. You love it.
You praise its legs to a buyer for half an hour. He buys it to make you stop.
You learn more about lying in an afternoon than in a year of murim politics.

events.text: Your ugly pony from the horse fair can run. Not fast, but forever: it trots all day and all night and never tires. A courier of the frontier post sees it and offers you a fortune.

effects.log: You refuse. The pony bites the courier, which settles it.

choices.text: Lend it to the post for a season

effects.log: It carries a message across the steppe faster than anything. The post pays you well.

events.text: The ugly pony from the horse fair is old now, grey round the muzzle, still bad-tempered. At the horse fair this year, the boy who sold it to you, grown up, sees it and laughs until he cries.

effects.log: He listens, amazed. He swears he will never judge a horse by its looks again. He will, of course.
It does, with relish. It is the happiest you have seen it in years.

events.text: On a beach of the eastern coast, the shells hum when the tide goes out: a soft, high, endless sound like children singing far away. A fisher boy says it is the voices of the sea people, counting.

choices.text: Hold a shell to your ear

effects.log: It sings a single note, and then, you swear, a second one.
You fill a basket. At home they hum quietly together all night.

choices.text: Run along the shore with the boy

effects.log: You race the tide together. You lose. You do not care.

events.text: The fisher boy of the singing beach has found that the shells sing louder before a storm, a day or two before, enough to warn the boats. But nobody in the village will believe a boy and some shells.

ok.log: You stand on the beach with them while the shells scream. They keep the boats in. The storm comes. Nobody is lost.

fail.log: They laugh. But the boy's mother keeps her husband's boat in, and he is the only one not caught out.

choices.text: Sit with the boy and listen

effects.log: You listen together for a day. When the shells go loud, you run to every house yourself.

events.text: The fishing village of the singing beach keeps a basket of shells at the harbour mouth now, and a grown fisher listens to them every dawn: the boy, now the harbour master, very serious about it.

effects.log: The shells sing softly: a fair day. He nods, satisfied, and sends the boats out.

choices.text: Give him your basket of shells

effects.log: Your shells join his. The singing is louder. The village is safer.

events.text: In a valley of the Western Regions, apricot trees bloom so thick the whole valley is pink, and the only people there are an old couple who say they planted every tree themselves, one a year, for sixty years.

effects.log: You pick apricots for a week. Your fingers are sticky and your heart is light.
They lead you to a gnarled old tree in the middle. "Our wedding," they say together.
You sleep in the pink shade all afternoon.

events.text: The old couple of the apricot valley are worried: a caravan route is being planned through their valley, and the road builders want to cut down the trees. They are too old to argue.

ok.log: You show the surveyor the valley in bloom. The road goes round the hill. It is longer, and nobody minds.

fail.log: They will not change the route, but they agree to plant two trees for every one they cut.

choices.text: Plant new trees along the new road

effects.log: You plant a line of saplings along the planned road. The caravans will have shade.

events.text: The old couple of the apricot valley have both died, within a week of each other. They are buried under the first tree. The valley is in bloom, and caravans have stopped on the road to look.

effects.log: You plant one more. Sixty-one. The caravan drivers help.
You tell it. A camel driver, a big rough man, has to turn away.

events.text: On a hillside a long kiln climbs the slope like a dragon, a hundred paces of brick, and once a year it is fired for seven days. The potters need every hand to feed it wood day and night.

choices.text: Shape a bowl of your own to fire

effects.log: Your bowl is lumpy. The potters put it in anyway, at the hottest end.

choices.text: Feed the kiln for a night

effects.log: Heat like a furnace. Sweat, sparks, songs. You fall asleep at dawn on a pile of wood.

choices.text: Watch the fire from a distance

effects.log: At night the kiln glows through its bricks like a sleeping dragon.

events.text: On the seventh day the dragon kiln is opened. The potters pull out a thousand pots, and among them a lumpy bowl glazed a colour nobody has ever seen: a blue like the sky after rain.

effects.log: Nobody knows. The head potter turns it in his hands for an hour, and then asks to keep it.
You drink tea from it every morning. It makes the tea taste like a clear day.

events.text: The potters of the dragon kiln have been trying for years to make the sky blue again. This year the head potter sends for you: the colour has come back, and he wants the person whose clumsy hands first made it to open the kiln.

effects.log: Inside, a hundred bowls the colour of the sky after rain. The potters weep. You are very proud of your lumps.
He opens it. The blue is perfect. He brings you the first bowl anyway.

events.text: High on a mountain path you find a small child sitting on a rock, quite calm, eating a pear. The child says their name is Little Pear, they live at the top, and they came down to see what the bottom looks like.

effects.log: At the top there is a temple, and a frantic old abbot who has searched all night.
You walk down to the village. The child is unimpressed with the bottom, but likes the noodles.

events.text: Little Pear of the mountain temple has come down again, and this time brought you a gift from the abbot: a jar of pears preserved in honey, and a request that you visit.

effects.log: The abbot gives you tea and asks you to teach Little Pear about the world at the bottom, now and then.
They are the best pears you have ever eaten. You go up to say thank you anyway.

events.text: Little Pear is grown, a young monk who has decided to leave the mountain and see the whole world, not just the bottom of it. The abbot asks you to walk the first day with them.

effects.log: You walk down together, talking. At the bottom, Little Pear thanks you and walks off towards the horizon.

choices.text: Give them a map and a pear

effects.log: You give them both. Little Pear laughs and eats the pear first.

events.text: In the paddies at night, the frogs sing so loudly the village cannot sleep. An old man insists they sing in tune and that he has been conducting them for years. He has a stick. He waves it. The frogs, oddly, seem to follow.

effects.log: He conducts for an hour. The frogs rise and fall with his stick. You cannot explain it.
The frogs go silent and stare at you. Then they all start again at once.

choices.text: Go to sleep with cotton in your ears

effects.log: You sleep well. You dream of frogs in robes.

events.text: The frog conductor is ill, and the frogs of the paddies are singing out of time, all night, wildly. The village begs you to take the stick.

ok.log: After a hopeless hour, they follow you. The village sleeps. You do not, but you are proud.

fail.log: They ignore you entirely. But the old man, hearing the chaos from his bed, laughs so hard he feels better.

choices.text: Carry the old man out to the paddies

effects.log: You carry him out in his blanket. He waves the stick from your arms. The frogs obey.

events.text: The village of the frog choir holds a summer concert in the paddies now: the old man's granddaughter conducts, the frogs sing, and people come from three villages to listen and laugh and wave their own sticks.

choices.text: Bring a stick of your own

effects.log: You conduct one corner of the paddy. Your frogs come in late every time. The crowd adores them.
It is, against all reason, music.

events.text: On a forest road, bandits step out with knives, then stop, and ask you very politely whether you could spare a little silver, because they are new at this and their village is starving.

effects.log: They thank you and bow. One gives you a receipt, written very carefully.

ok.log: You disarm them all in a breath. They apologise at length.

fail.log: They are bad bandits but there are a lot of them. They take your silver, apologising.

choices.text: Ask what has happened to their village

effects.log: A flood took the rice. The landlord took the rest.

events.text: You pass through the polite bandits' village. It is as bad as they said: thin children, a broken dyke, and the landlord's tax collector at the gate with soldiers.

ok.log: You quote the imperial law on flood relief at him. He goes away, pale.

fail.log: He laughs. But when the soldiers see you, they lose interest in collecting anything today.

effects.log: You haul stones for a month with the former bandits. The dyke is better than before.

events.text: The village of the polite bandits has had a good harvest. On the forest road, the same men step out of the trees, and hold out not knives but a bag of silver for you: repayment, with interest, and a carefully written receipt.

effects.log: You take it. They are as proud as if they had won a war.

choices.text: Tell them to keep it for a bad year

effects.log: They argue for an hour, then agree, and name the fund after you.

events.text: On a frozen mountain lake, an old woman sits by a hole in the ice with a line, a small fire and a kettle. She has caught nothing, she says cheerfully, for three winters, and has never been happier.

effects.log: You fish all day. Nothing bites. She makes you tea. The silence of the ice is huge and kind.
You cut a wide clean hole. She thanks you, and goes on catching nothing in it.
"For the waiting," she says. "The fish are a distraction."

events.text: You come back to the frozen lake. The old ice fisher has caught something at last: a huge old pike, as long as your arm, and she is looking at it in great dismay, because now she has to decide what to do with it.

effects.log: You slide it back into the hole. It hangs in the dark water, looking up, then goes. She is relieved.
You cook it over her little fire. It is wonderful. She says she will never catch another, and seems glad.

events.text: The old ice fisher has left the frozen lake for good: too old for the cold, her nephew says. But at her hole in the ice someone has left her stool, her kettle and her line, for whoever comes next.

effects.log: You catch nothing all day. You find you do not mind at all.
